Path compression shortens future finds, and union by size keeps the trees shallow.Reading the N × N matrix takes O(N^2) time. DSU operations take amortized O(α(N)) each, so the full time complexity is O(N^2 α(N) + M α(N)); space complexity is O(N). The scanner consumes whitespace rather than splitting individual lines, so arbitrary spaces and line breaks are handled.import java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int cityCount = input.nextInt(); int planLength = input.nextInt(); DisjointSet dsu = new DisjointSet(cityCount); for (int from = 0; from &lt; cityCount; from++) { for (int to = 0; to &lt; cityCount; to++) { if (input.nextInt() == 1) { dsu.union(from, to); } } } int firstCity = input.nextInt() - 1; int representative = dsu.find(firstCity); for (int i = 1; i &lt; planLength; i++) { int city = input.nextInt() - 1; if (dsu.find(city) != representative) { System.out.println("NO"); return; } } System.out.println("YES"); } private static final class DisjointSet { private final int[] parent; private final int[] size; DisjointSet(int n) { parent = new int[n]; size = new int[n]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { parent[i] = i; size[i] = 1; } } int find(int city) { if (parent[city] != city) { parent[city] = find(parent[city]); } return parent[city]; } void union(int a, int b) { int rootA = find(a); int rootB = find(b); if (rootA == rootB) return; if (size[rootA] &lt; size[rootB]) { int temp = rootA; rootA = rootB; rootB = temp; } parent[rootB] = rootA; size[rootA] += size[rootB]; } } private static final class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length; private int position; private int read() throws IOException { if (position == length) { length = input.read(buffer); position = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[position++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } }}

title: BOJ. Merge Files (11066)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, BOJ, Dynamic Programming, Merge Files, 파일 합치기
snippet: ProblemThe cost of merging two adjacent files is the sum of their sizes. After every merge, the result remains in the same sequence, so an optimal plan can be split at its final merge: the files in [i, k] are merged first, the files in [k + 1, j] are merged separately, and those two results are merged for a cost equal to the total size of [i, j].Let dp[i][j] be the minimum cost to merge files i through j (zero-based, inclusive), and let prefix contain prefix sums of file sizes. Then:dp[i][i] = 0dp[i][j] = prefix[j + 1] - prefix[i] + min(dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j]), i &lt;= k &lt; jThe interval sum is computed in constant time from the prefix sums. A direct search over every split takes O(K^3) time. Here each file size is positive, so the interval-sum cost satisfies the quadrangle inequality and is monotone with interval inclusion. The resulting optimal split points satisfy the Knuth monotonicity invariant:opt[i][j - 1] &lt;= opt[i][j] &lt;= opt[i + 1][j]Therefore, when computing dp[i][j], it is sufficient to inspect split points from opt[i][j - 1] through opt[i + 1][j], inclusive, rather than the full interval. Initialize opt[i][i] = i; process intervals in increasing length so both neighboring optima have already been computed. Selecting the first minimum in each interval gives a consistent opt table. This reduces the total running time to O(K^2), with O(K^2) space for dp and opt (and O(K) for prefix sums). long is used for all costs and prefix sums.import java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int testCases = input.nextInt(); StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); while (testCases-- &gt; 0) { int k = input.nextInt(); long[] prefix = new long[k + 1]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; k; i++) { prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + input.nextInt(); } long[][] dp = new long[k][k]; int[][] opt = new int[k][k]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; k; i++) { opt[i][i] = i; } for (int length = 2; length &lt;= k; length++) { for (int i = 0; i + length &lt;= k; i++) { int j = i + length - 1; int firstSplit = opt[i][j - 1]; int lastSplit = opt[i + 1][j]; long intervalSize = prefix[j + 1] - prefix[i]; long best = Long.MAX_VALUE; int bestSplit = firstSplit; for (int split = firstSplit; split &lt;= lastSplit; split++) { long cost = dp[i][split] + dp[split + 1][j] + intervalSize; if (cost &lt; best) { best = cost; bestSplit = split; } } dp[i][j] = best; opt[i][j] = bestSplit; } } output.append(dp[0][k - 1]).append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); } private static final class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length; private int position; private int read() throws IOException { if (position == length) { length = input.read(buffer); position = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[position++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } }}

title: BOJ. Exercise (1956)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, BOJ, Dijkstra, Floyd Warshall Graph, Exercise, 운동
snippet: Problem linkLet dist[u][v] be the shortest known directed distance from vertex u to vertex v. Initialize every entry to infinity, set dist[i][i] = 0, and record the minimum weight among parallel direct edges. Keeping the diagonal at zero makes the empty path available to Floyd–Warshall; direct self-loops are retained separately as edges for cycle evaluation.Floyd–Warshall considers each vertex k as an allowed intermediate vertex. For each pair (u, v), a shortest route either avoids k or goes from u to k and then from k to v, so update dist[u][v] with dist[u][k] + dist[k][v]. Skip the addition if either partial route is unreachable. Afterward, every directed edge u -&gt; v with weight w closes a cycle exactly when a route exists from v back to u; that cycle has length w + dist[v][u]. Taking the minimum over all edges finds the shortest cycle. If no edge has a return route, there is no cycle and the answer is -1. This also handles a self-loop (u == v) and parallel edges.The Floyd–Warshall phase takes O(V^3) time, and scanning the edge matrix takes O(V^2) time. The distance and edge matrices use O(V^2) space. long distances and an infinity sentinel of Long.MAX_VALUE / 4 leave ample room for sums; unreachable partial paths are checked before addition.import java.io.*;import java.util.*;public class Main { static class FastScanner { private final InputStream input; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length = 0; private int pointer = 0; FastScanner(InputStream input) { this.input = input; } private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = input.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[pointer++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(System.in); int v = input.nextInt(); int e = input.nextInt(); long infinity = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4; long[][] edge = new long[v][v]; long[][] dist = new long[v][v]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; v; i++) { Arrays.fill(edge[i], infinity); Arrays.fill(dist[i], infinity); dist[i][i] = 0; } for (int i = 0; i &lt; e; i++) { int from = input.nextInt() - 1; int to = input.nextInt() - 1; long weight = input.nextInt(); edge[from][to] = Math.min(edge[from][to], weight); dist[from][to] = Math.min(dist[from][to], weight); } for (int mid = 0; mid &lt; v; mid++) { for (int from = 0; from &lt; v; from++) { if (dist[from][mid] == infinity) continue; for (int to = 0; to &lt; v; to++) { if (dist[mid][to] == infinity) continue; dist[from][to] = Math.min( dist[from][to], dist[from][mid] + dist[mid][to]); } } } long answer = infinity; for (int from = 0; from &lt; v; from++) { for (int to = 0; to &lt; v; to++) { if (edge[from][to] == infinity || dist[to][from] == infinity) continue; answer = Math.min(answer, edge[from][to] + dist[to][from]); } } System.out.println(answer == infinity ? -1 : answer); }}

title: BOJ. KCM Travel (10217)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, BOJ, Dijkstra, Graph, KCM Travel, Review, difficult
snippet: ApproachLet best[v][c] be the minimum travel time to reach airport v with total cost at most c. Initialize every entry to infinity except best[0][c] = 0 for every budget c, since the start is reachable without spending any money. For each ticket, consider the new cost and relax only if it is within M. When a route improves a budget entry, propagate that time to larger budgets until an existing entry is already as good; more available budget cannot make the best time worse.Run Dijkstra’s algorithm over these (airport, cost) states. The priority queue is ordered by travel time using Integer.compare, avoiding subtraction overflow. Skip a state if its time is greater than the best time for its budget; a cheaper route with less spending dominates it. Stop when the destination is popped: all ticket times are nonnegative, so this is the minimum travel time among all budget-feasible routes. Create the graph, table, and queue inside each test case so no state leaks between cases.The invariant is that each finite entry is the best time found for its airport under that budget, and each queued state is a feasible route at its recorded cost. Relaxation checks every next ticket within the input budget; propagating improvements to larger budgets preserves the at-most-budget meaning. Since ticket times are nonnegative, Dijkstra’s minimum-time extraction finalizes feasible routes in order. Thus, the first non-stale destination state popped has minimum travel time among all budget-feasible routes.There are at most N(M + 1) table states, so the table uses O(NM) space. With K ticket edges, sparse-state priority-queue work is approximately O(K log(NM)); in the worst case, tickets may be examined from many budget states, giving an explicit bound of O(KM log(NM)).Problem linkJavaimport java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;import java.util.ArrayList;import java.util.Arrays;import java.util.List;import java.util.PriorityQueue;public class Main { private static class Ticket { final int destination; final int cost; final int time; Ticket(int destination, int cost, int time) { this.destination = destination; this.cost = cost; this.time = time; } } private static class State { final int airport; final int cost; final int time; State(int airport, int cost, int time) { this.airport = airport; this.cost = cost; this.time = time; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int testCases = input.nextInt(); StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int testCase = 0; testCase &lt; testCases; testCase++) { int airportCount = input.nextInt(); int budget = input.nextInt(); int ticketCount = input.nextInt(); List&lt;Ticket&gt;[] graph = new ArrayList[airportCount]; for (int airport = 0; airport &lt; airportCount; airport++) { graph[airport] = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(); } for (int i = 0; i &lt; ticketCount; i++) { int from = input.nextInt() - 1; int to = input.nextInt() - 1; int cost = input.nextInt(); int time = input.nextInt(); graph[from].add(new Ticket(to, cost, time)); } int[][] best = new int[airportCount][budget + 1]; for (int[] times : best) { Arrays.fill(times, Integer.MAX_VALUE); } for (int budgetLimit = 0; budgetLimit &lt;= budget; budgetLimit++) { best[0][budgetLimit] = 0; } PriorityQueue&lt;State&gt; queue = new PriorityQueue&lt;&gt;( (left, right) -&gt; Integer.compare(left.time, right.time)); queue.add(new State(0, 0, 0)); int answer = -1; while (!queue.isEmpty()) { State current = queue.poll(); if (current.time &gt; best[current.airport][current.cost]) { continue; } if (current.airport == airportCount - 1) { answer = current.time; break; } for (Ticket ticket : graph[current.airport]) { int nextCost = current.cost + ticket.cost; if (nextCost &gt; budget) { continue; } int nextTime = current.time + ticket.time; if (nextTime &lt; best[ticket.destination][nextCost]) { for (int limit = nextCost; limit &lt;= budget; limit++) { if (nextTime &gt;= best[ticket.destination][limit]) { break; } best[ticket.destination][limit] = nextTime; } queue.add(new State(ticket.destination, nextCost, nextTime)); } } } if (answer == -1) { output.append("Poor KCM\n"); } else { output.append(answer).append('\n'); } } System.out.print(output); } private static class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int position; private int length; private int read() throws IOException { if (position == length) { length = input.read(buffer); position = 0; if (length == -1) { return -1; } } return buffer[position++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } }}

title: BOJ. Floyd (11404)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, BOJ, Floyd-Warshall, 플로이드 워셜, Graph, 플로이드, Review
snippet: Problem linkLet dist[i][j] be the shortest known cost from city i to city j. Initially, the only known routes are staying in the same city (cost zero) and the direct bus routes. If several routes have the same endpoints, keep only the cheapest one.Process each city k as a possible intermediate stop. When considering k, dist[i][j] is the shortest route from i to j whose intermediate cities are among those already processed. The new best route either does not use k, or consists of a route from i to k followed by one from k to j; thus update with dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]. Skip the addition when either part is unreachable so the infinity sentinel is never added to a distance. After all intermediate cities have been processed, every shortest route is represented.There are three nested loops over the N cities, so the time complexity is O(N^3). The distance matrix uses O(N^2) space. A long matrix and a large sentinel safely represent unreachable pairs and path sums. The required output uses 0 for pairs with no route.import java.io.*;import java.util.*;public class Main { static class FastScanner { private final InputStream input; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length = 0; private int pointer = 0; FastScanner(InputStream input) { this.input = input; } private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = input.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[pointer++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(System.in); int n = input.nextInt(); int m = input.nextInt(); long infinity = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4; long[][] dist = new long[n][n]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { Arrays.fill(dist[i], infinity); dist[i][i] = 0; } for (int i = 0; i &lt; m; i++) { int from = input.nextInt() - 1; int to = input.nextInt() - 1; long cost = input.nextInt(); dist[from][to] = Math.min(dist[from][to], cost); } for (int mid = 0; mid &lt; n; mid++) { for (int from = 0; from &lt; n; from++) { if (dist[from][mid] == infinity) continue; for (int to = 0; to &lt; n; to++) { if (dist[mid][to] == infinity) continue; dist[from][to] = Math.min( dist[from][to], dist[from][mid] + dist[mid][to]); } } } StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int from = 0; from &lt; n; from++) { for (int to = 0; to &lt; n; to++) { if (to &gt; 0) output.append(' '); output.append(dist[from][to] == infinity ? 0 : dist[from][to]); } output.append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); }}

title: LeetCode. 997. Find the Town Judge
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Find the Town Judge
snippet: Problem linkDegree characterizationTreat each trust pair [a, b] as a directed edge from person a to person b. A town judge trusts nobody, so their outdegree is 0. Everyone else trusts the judge, so their indegree is n - 1. Both conditions are necessary: an incoming-edge count alone could identify someone who also trusts another person.Count incoming and outgoing edges for every person, then return the person satisfying both conditions. For n == 1, the sole person has indegree and outdegree zero; they meet the conditions precisely when there are no trust edges, so the same scan handles this edge case without a special branch. If nobody meets both conditions, return -1.Each trust pair is processed once and each person is checked once, giving O(n + m) time for m = trust.length. The two degree arrays use O(n) extra space.class Solution { public int findJudge(int n, int[][] trust) { int[] indegree = new int[n + 1]; int[] outdegree = new int[n + 1]; for (int[] relation : trust) { outdegree[relation[0]]++; indegree[relation[1]]++; } for (int person = 1; person &lt;= n; person++) { if (outdegree[person] == 0 &amp;&amp; indegree[person] == n - 1) { return person; } } return -1; }}

title: BOJ. Time Machine (11657)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, BOJ, Bellman Ford, 벨만 포드, Graph, Time Machine, 타임머신, Review
snippet: ApproachThe graph is directed and may contain negative edge weights, so Dijkstra’s algorithm is not suitable. Bellman–Ford stores the best known distance from vertex 1 and relaxes every edge up to V - 1 times. Any shortest path without a cycle uses at most V - 1 edges; stopping when a pass makes no changes avoids unnecessary work.Initialize all distances to a true long infinity value and set only vertex 1 to zero. Before relaxing an edge, skip it if its source is still infinite. This both prevents arithmetic on the sentinel and ensures that an unreachable negative cycle cannot be mistaken for a cycle reachable from vertex 1. After the passes, one more scan detects a reachable negative cycle: if any edge can still be relaxed from a finite distance, print -1. Otherwise, print the distances to vertices 2 through N, using -1 for unreachable vertices.Bellman–Ford supports negative edges. Its worst-case time complexity is O(VE) and its space complexity is O(V + E).Problem linkJavaimport java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;import java.util.ArrayList;import java.util.Arrays;import java.util.List;public class Main { private static final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4; private static class Edge { final int from; final int to; final long weight; Edge(int from, int to, long weight) { this.from = from; this.to = to; this.weight = weight; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int vertexCount = input.nextInt(); int edgeCount = input.nextInt(); List&lt;Edge&gt; edges = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(edgeCount); for (int i = 0; i &lt; edgeCount; i++) { int from = input.nextInt() - 1; int to = input.nextInt() - 1; long weight = input.nextLong(); edges.add(new Edge(from, to, weight)); } long[] distance = new long[vertexCount]; Arrays.fill(distance, INF); distance[0] = 0; for (int pass = 0; pass &lt; vertexCount - 1; pass++) { boolean changed = false; for (Edge edge : edges) { if (distance[edge.from] == INF) { continue; } long candidate = distance[edge.from] + edge.weight; if (candidate &lt; distance[edge.to]) { distance[edge.to] = candidate; changed = true; } } if (!changed) { break; } } for (Edge edge : edges) { if (distance[edge.from] != INF &amp;&amp; distance[edge.from] + edge.weight &lt; distance[edge.to]) { System.out.println(-1); return; } } StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int vertex = 1; vertex &lt; vertexCount; vertex++) { output.append(distance[vertex] == INF ? -1 : distance[vertex]).append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); } private static class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int position; private int length; private int read() throws IOException { if (position == length) { length = input.read(buffer); position = 0; if (length == -1) { return -1; } } return buffer[position++]; } private long nextLong() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); boolean negative = c == '-'; if (negative) { c = read(); } long value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return negative ? -value : value; } private int nextInt() throws IOException { return (int) nextLong(); } }}

title: BOJ. Unidentified destination (9370)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, BOJ, Dijkstra, Graph, Unidentified destination, 미확인 도착지, Review
snippet: Problem linkApproachFor each test case, run Dijkstra from the source s and from both endpoints g and h of the designated edge. A candidate destination x qualifies exactly when some shortest route from s to x can use that edge. Its shortest distance must therefore equal one of these two route lengths: dist(s, g) + w(g, h) + dist(h, x) dist(s, h) + w(g, h) + dist(g, x)The two expressions cover both directions of travel across the undirected g-h edge. If several parallel edges connect g and h, use their minimum weight: any heavier parallel edge cannot make a shortest route, while the minimum one is available in the graph. An unreachable segment makes that expression invalid, so check for INF before adding distances.For correctness, if a shortest route uses g-h, its prefix to the first endpoint and suffix from the other endpoint must themselves be shortest; otherwise replacing either part would produce a shorter route. Its total length is therefore one of the two expressions above. Conversely, if either expression equals dist(s, x), concatenating those shortest segments with the g-h edge gives a shortest route that uses the edge.The graph is stored as an adjacency list, and Dijkstra uses a min-priority queue with lazy deletion. Distances and edge weights are long; Long.compare orders queue entries without subtraction overflow. Candidates are sorted numerically before output. The time complexity per test case is O((V + E) log V + C log C), where C is the number of candidates; space complexity is O(V + E).Javaimport java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;import java.util.ArrayList;import java.util.Arrays;import java.util.Collections;import java.util.List;import java.util.PriorityQueue;public class Main { private static final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4; public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int testCases = input.nextInt(); StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int testCase = 0; testCase &lt; testCases; testCase++) { int n = input.nextInt(); int m = input.nextInt(); int candidateCount = input.nextInt(); int source = input.nextInt() - 1; int g = input.nextInt() - 1; int h = input.nextInt() - 1; List&lt;Edge&gt;[] graph = new ArrayList[n]; for (int vertex = 0; vertex &lt; n; vertex++) { graph[vertex] = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(); } long ghWeight = INF; for (int i = 0; i &lt; m; i++) { int a = input.nextInt() - 1; int b = input.nextInt() - 1; long weight = input.nextLong(); graph[a].add(new Edge(b, weight)); graph[b].add(new Edge(a, weight)); if ((a == g &amp;&amp; b == h) || (a == h &amp;&amp; b == g)) { ghWeight = Math.min(ghWeight, weight); } } long[] fromSource = dijkstra(graph, source); long[] fromG = dijkstra(graph, g); long[] fromH = dijkstra(graph, h); List&lt;Integer&gt; candidates = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(candidateCount); for (int i = 0; i &lt; candidateCount; i++) { int candidate = input.nextInt() - 1; long shortest = fromSource[candidate]; if (shortest != INF &amp;&amp; ghWeight != INF &amp;&amp; (equalsRoute(shortest, fromSource[g], ghWeight, fromH[candidate]) || equalsRoute(shortest, fromSource[h], ghWeight, fromG[candidate]))) { candidates.add(candidate + 1); } } Collections.sort(candidates); for (int candidate : candidates) { output.append(candidate).append(' '); } output.append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); } private static boolean equalsRoute(long shortest, long first, long edge, long last) { return first != INF &amp;&amp; edge != INF &amp;&amp; last != INF &amp;&amp; shortest == first + edge + last; } private static long[] dijkstra(List&lt;Edge&gt;[] graph, int start) { long[] distance = new long[graph.length]; Arrays.fill(distance, INF); distance[start] = 0; PriorityQueue&lt;State&gt; queue = new PriorityQueue&lt;&gt;( (left, right) -&gt; Long.compare(left.distance, right.distance)); queue.offer(new State(start, 0)); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { State current = queue.poll(); if (current.distance != distance[current.vertex]) { continue; } for (Edge edge : graph[current.vertex]) { long nextDistance = current.distance + edge.weight; if (nextDistance &lt; distance[edge.to]) { distance[edge.to] = nextDistance; queue.offer(new State(edge.to, nextDistance)); } } } return distance; } private static class Edge { final int to; final long weight; Edge(int to, long weight) { this.to = to; this.weight = weight; } } private static class State { final int vertex; final long distance; State(int vertex, long distance) { this.vertex = vertex; this.distance = distance; } } private static class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int position; private int length; private int read() throws IOException { if (position == length) { length = input.read(buffer); position = 0; if (length == -1) { return -1; } } return buffer[position++]; } long nextLong() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); long value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } int nextInt() throws IOException { return (int) nextLong(); } }}

title: LeetCode. 312. Burst Balloons
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Dynamic Programming, Burst Balloons, Review
snippet: ProblemInterval dynamic programmingAdd a virtual balloon with value 1 at each end of the array. Let dp[l][r] be the maximum coins obtainable by bursting every balloon strictly between boundaries l and r, while leaving those two boundary balloons unburst.Choose the last balloon k to burst in that open interval. At that moment, all other balloons inside the interval are already gone, so its neighbors are exactly l and r. The final burst earns values[l] * values[k] * values[r]; the balloons on either side were burst earlier and contribute the independently optimal subproblems dp[l][k] and dp[k][r]. Thus:dp[l][r] = max(dp[l][k] + values[l] * values[k] * values[r] + dp[k][r])for l &lt; k &lt; r. Evaluate intervals in increasing width so both smaller intervals have already been computed. With n original balloons there are O(n^2) intervals and up to O(n) choices of k per interval, giving O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space. An empty input has no interior balloons, so the answer is zero.class Solution { public int maxCoins(int[] nums) { int n = nums.length; int[] values = new int[n + 2]; values[0] = values[n + 1] = 1; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { values[i + 1] = nums[i]; } int[][] dp = new int[n + 2][n + 2]; for (int width = 2; width &lt; n + 2; width++) { for (int left = 0; left + width &lt; n + 2; left++) { int right = left + width; for (int last = left + 1; last &lt; right; last++) { int coins = dp[left][last] + values[left] * values[last] * values[right] + dp[last][right]; dp[left][right] = Math.max(dp[left][right], coins); } } } return dp[0][n + 1]; }}

title: BOJ. Shortest path with specification (1504)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, BOJ, Dijkstra, Graph, Shortest path with specification, 특정한 최단 경로
snippet: [Link] https://www.acmicpc.net/problem/1504ApproachIn an undirected graph with positive edge weights, find the shortest route from vertex 1 to vertex N that visits both required vertices v1 and v2. There are only two possible orders: 1 → v1 → v2 → N and 1 → v2 → v1 → N. Add the shortest distance for each segment in both orders, then choose the smaller reachable route. If neither route is reachable, print -1.Run Dijkstra’s algorithm from vertex 1, v1, and v2. The two candidate lengths are d(1,v1) + d(v1,v2) + d(v2,N) and d(1,v2) + d(v2,v1) + d(v1,N). Because the graph is undirected, d(v1,v2) = d(v2,v1). If a required vertex is the start or end, the corresponding segment naturally has distance zero.Use long for distances and candidate sums, and do not add a candidate if any segment is unreachable. Dijkstra discards stale priority-queue entries when their distance no longer matches the best known distance. The time complexity is O((V + E) log V) and the space complexity is O(V + E).Javaimport java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;import java.util.ArrayList;import java.util.Arrays;import java.util.List;import java.util.PriorityQueue;public class Main { private static final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4; public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int n = input.nextInt(); int e = input.nextInt(); List&lt;Edge&gt;[] graph = new ArrayList[n]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { graph[i] = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(); } for (int i = 0; i &lt; e; i++) { int a = input.nextInt() - 1; int b = input.nextInt() - 1; long weight = input.nextLong(); graph[a].add(new Edge(b, weight)); graph[b].add(new Edge(a, weight)); } int v1 = input.nextInt() - 1; int v2 = input.nextInt() - 1; long[] fromStart = dijkstra(graph, 0); long[] fromV1 = dijkstra(graph, v1); long[] fromV2 = dijkstra(graph, v2); long viaV1ThenV2 = routeLength( fromStart[v1], fromV1[v2], fromV2[n - 1]); long viaV2ThenV1 = routeLength( fromStart[v2], fromV2[v1], fromV1[n - 1]); long answer = Math.min(viaV1ThenV2, viaV2ThenV1); System.out.println(answer == INF ? -1 : answer); } private static long[] dijkstra(List&lt;Edge&gt;[] graph, int start) { long[] distance = new long[graph.length]; Arrays.fill(distance, INF); distance[start] = 0; PriorityQueue&lt;State&gt; queue = new PriorityQueue&lt;&gt;(); queue.offer(new State(start, 0)); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { State current = queue.poll(); if (current.distance != distance[current.vertex]) { continue; } for (Edge edge : graph[current.vertex]) { long nextDistance = current.distance + edge.weight; if (nextDistance &lt; distance[edge.to]) { distance[edge.to] = nextDistance; queue.offer(new State(edge.to, nextDistance)); } } } return distance; } private static long routeLength(long first, long middle, long last) { if (first == INF || middle == INF || last == INF) { return INF; } return first + middle + last; } private static class Edge { final int to; final long weight; Edge(int to, long weight) { this.to = to; this.weight = weight; } } private static class State implements Comparable&lt;State&gt; { final int vertex; final long distance; State(int vertex, long distance) { this.vertex = vertex; this.distance = distance; } @Override public int compareTo(State other) { return Long.compare(distance, other.distance); } } private static class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream in = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int index; private int size; private int read() throws IOException { if (index == size) { size = in.read(buffer); index = 0; if (size == -1) { return -1; } } return buffer[index++]; } long nextLong() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); long value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } int nextInt() throws IOException { return (int) nextLong(); } }}

title: BOJ. Prefix Product (11505)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, Segment Tree, BOJ, Prefix Product, 구간 곱 구하기
snippet: ProblemMaintain an array under point assignments and answer the product of any inclusive range modulo 1,000,000,007. Since an update changes only one position, an iterative segment tree can recompute just the ancestors of that leaf. Each internal node stores the product of its two children modulo MOD.The tree uses n leaves at indices [n, 2n). To assign index p, replace leaf p + n, then walk upward and recompute each parent. For a query [left, right], convert it to the half-open interval [left + n, right + n + 1). At each level, consume a left boundary node when it is a right child and a right boundary node when it is a left child; then move both boundaries to their parents. This visits only the canonical tree nodes covering the requested interval, including either endpoint exactly once.Multiplication modulo MOD has identity 1, so both query accumulators start at 1; this also makes the result of a single-element range and ranges containing zero correct. Assignments store the new value directly, including 0—there is no division or special zero bookkeeping. Cast one factor to long before multiplying, since two values below MOD can overflow a 32-bit integer. The tree is built in O(N) time, each point assignment and range query takes O(log N), and the tree uses O(N) space.import java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;public class Main { private static final int MOD = 1_000_000_007; public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int n = input.nextInt(); int updates = input.nextInt(); int queries = input.nextInt(); int operationCount = updates + queries; int[] tree = new int[2 * n]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { tree[n + i] = input.nextInt(); } for (int node = n - 1; node &gt; 0; node--) { tree[node] = multiply(tree[node &lt;&lt; 1], tree[node &lt;&lt; 1 | 1]); } StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i &lt; operationCount; i++) { int type = input.nextInt(); int b = input.nextInt(); int c = input.nextInt(); if (type == 1) { set(tree, n, b - 1, c); } else { output.append(product(tree, n, b - 1, c)).append('\n'); } } System.out.print(output); } private static int multiply(int a, int b) { return (int) ((long) a * b % MOD); } private static void set(int[] tree, int n, int index, int value) { int node = n + index; tree[node] = value; while ((node &gt;&gt;= 1) &gt; 0) { tree[node] = multiply(tree[node &lt;&lt; 1], tree[node &lt;&lt; 1 | 1]); } } // Returns the product on the zero-based inclusive interval [left, right]. private static int product(int[] tree, int n, int left, int right) { int l = left + n; int r = right + n + 1; int leftProduct = 1; int rightProduct = 1; while (l &lt; r) { if ((l &amp; 1) != 0) leftProduct = multiply(leftProduct, tree[l++]); if ((r &amp; 1) != 0) rightProduct = multiply(tree[--r], rightProduct); l &gt;&gt;= 1; r &gt;&gt;= 1; } return multiply(leftProduct, rightProduct); } private static final class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length; private int position; private int read() throws IOException { if (position == length) { length = input.read(buffer); position = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[position++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } }}

title: BOJ. Shortest Path (1753)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, BOJ, DFS, Shortest Path, 최단경로
snippet: SolutionThe graph is directed, so each edge is stored only in the adjacency list of its source. Dijkstra’s algorithm is valid because all edge weights are nonnegative. The distance array stores the best known distance from the source; when an entry with the smallest tentative distance is removed from the priority queue, relaxing its outgoing edges can only improve neighbors’ distances. If a better route is found later, a new queue entry is added. Older entries are discarded when their distance no longer matches the array.The queue comparator uses Long.compare rather than subtraction to avoid overflow. Distances use long; unreachable vertices retain INF and are printed as INF, while the source is printed as 0. Parallel edges are all retained, which does not change the result.With a lazy priority queue, the time complexity is O((V + E) log V) and the space complexity is O(V + E).Problem linkJavaimport java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;import java.util.ArrayList;import java.util.Arrays;import java.util.List;import java.util.PriorityQueue;public class Main { private static final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4; private static class Edge { final int to; final long weight; Edge(int to, long weight) { this.to = to; this.weight = weight; } } private static class State { final int vertex; final long distance; State(int vertex, long distance) { this.vertex = vertex; this.distance = distance; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int vertexCount = input.nextInt(); int edgeCount = input.nextInt(); int source = input.nextInt() - 1; List&lt;List&lt;Edge&gt;&gt; graph = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(vertexCount); for (int vertex = 0; vertex &lt; vertexCount; vertex++) { graph.add(new ArrayList&lt;&gt;()); } for (int i = 0; i &lt; edgeCount; i++) { int from = input.nextInt() - 1; int to = input.nextInt() - 1; long weight = input.nextLong(); graph.get(from).add(new Edge(to, weight)); } long[] distance = new long[vertexCount]; Arrays.fill(distance, INF); distance[source] = 0; PriorityQueue&lt;State&gt; queue = new PriorityQueue&lt;&gt;( (left, right) -&gt; Long.compare(left.distance, right.distance)); queue.add(new State(source, 0)); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { State current = queue.poll(); if (current.distance != distance[current.vertex]) { continue; } for (Edge edge : graph.get(current.vertex)) { long candidate = current.distance + edge.weight; if (candidate &lt; distance[edge.to]) { distance[edge.to] = candidate; queue.add(new State(edge.to, candidate)); } } } StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (long value : distance) { output.append(value == INF ? "INF" : value).append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); } private static class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int position; private int length; private int read() throws IOException { if (position == length) { length = input.read(buffer); position = 0; if (length == -1) { return -1; } } return buffer[position++]; } private long nextLong() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); boolean negative = c == '-'; if (negative) { c = read(); } long value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return negative ? -value : value; } private int nextInt() throws IOException { return (int) nextLong(); } }}

title: Programmers. Network
tags: Algorithm, JavaScript, Coding Interview, Programmers, Network, 네트워크, 프로그래머스
snippet: ProblemApproachThe computers form an undirected graph: computers[i][j] === 1 means computer i can connect directly to computer j. The requested number of networks is the number of connected components.Scan every computer. Whenever one has not yet been visited, it starts a new component. Mark it visited and use an explicit stack to visit every unvisited computer reachable through a connection. Mark each computer when it is pushed, so it can enter the stack only once. The diagonal entries represent links from a computer to itself; they do not discover another computer and are harmless because the current computer is already marked visited.This counts each component exactly once: the first unvisited computer encountered in a component starts its traversal, and that traversal marks every computer in that component. Afterward, none of its members can start another traversal. Conversely, every computer connected to that start is reached by repeatedly following edges, so no member of the component is missed.The adjacency matrix takes O(n²) time to inspect, and each computer is pushed and popped at most once. Thus total time is O(n²) and the auxiliary stack and visited array use O(n) space.JavaScriptfunction solution(n, computers) { const visited = new Array(n).fill(false); const stack = []; let networkCount = 0; for (let start = 0; start &lt; n; start++) { if (visited[start]) continue; networkCount++; visited[start] = true; stack.push(start); while (stack.length &gt; 0) { const current = stack.pop(); for (let next = 0; next &lt; n; next++) { if (computers[current][next] === 1 &amp;&amp; !visited[next]) { visited[next] = true; stack.push(next); } } } } return networkCount;}

title: BOJ. Bipartite Graph (1707)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, BOJ, DFS, Bipartite Graph, 이분 그래프
snippet: Color the vertices of each test graph with two colors. A graph is bipartite exactly when every edge joins vertices of different colors. The graph may be disconnected, so start a breadth-first search at every vertex that has not been colored yet. During the search, assign each newly discovered neighbor the opposite color. If an edge joins vertices that already have the same color, the graph is not bipartite; this also detects a self-loop.The invariant is that every processed edge connects opposite colors. BFS extends this valid two-way partition through each component; finding a same-color edge proves no such partition can satisfy all edges. Each vertex and edge is processed only a constant number of times, so the time complexity is O(V + E). The color and queue arrays use O(V) auxiliary space; the adjacency list uses O(V + E) space.Problem linkJavaimport java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int testCases = input.nextInt(); StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int test = 0; test &lt; testCases; test++) { int vertexCount = input.nextInt(); int edgeCount = input.nextInt(); int[] head = new int[vertexCount]; java.util.Arrays.fill(head, -1); int[] to = new int[2 * edgeCount]; int[] next = new int[2 * edgeCount]; for (int edge = 0; edge &lt; edgeCount; edge++) { int a = input.nextInt() - 1; int b = input.nextInt() - 1; to[2 * edge] = b; next[2 * edge] = head[a]; head[a] = 2 * edge; to[2 * edge + 1] = a; next[2 * edge + 1] = head[b]; head[b] = 2 * edge + 1; } int[] color = new int[vertexCount]; int[] queue = new int[vertexCount]; boolean bipartite = true; for (int start = 0; start &lt; vertexCount &amp;&amp; bipartite; start++) { if (color[start] != 0) { continue; } int front = 0; int back = 0; color[start] = 1; queue[back++] = start; while (front &lt; back &amp;&amp; bipartite) { int vertex = queue[front++]; for (int edge = head[vertex]; edge != -1; edge = next[edge]) { int neighbor = to[edge]; if (color[neighbor] == 0) { color[neighbor] = 3 - color[vertex]; queue[back++] = neighbor; } else if (color[neighbor] == color[vertex]) { bipartite = false; break; } } } } output.append(bipartite ? "YES\n" : "NO\n"); } System.out.print(output); } private static final class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length; private int position; private int read() throws IOException { if (position == length) { length = input.read(buffer); position = 0; if (length == -1) { return -1; } } return buffer[position++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } }}

title: BOJ. Move the Knight (7562)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, BOJ, DFS, Move the Knight, 나이트의 이동
snippet: Problem linkFor each test case, find the minimum number of knight moves between two squares on an L × L chessboard. Each move changes one coordinate by 1 and the other by 2, with either sign, and the knight must remain on the board.Treat every board square as a graph vertex and each legal knight move as an edge. Since all edges have equal cost, breadth-first search (BFS) visits squares in nondecreasing distance from the start. The first time the target is discovered therefore gives the shortest path length. The distance matrix also marks visited squares: a square is enqueued only while its distance is -1, so it enters the queue at most once. If start and target are the same square, the answer is zero.The input scanner accepts arbitrary whitespace, and the primitive queue is reused for every test case. A board has L² squares and at most eight outgoing moves per square, so the time complexity is O(L²) and the auxiliary space complexity is O(L²).import java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;public class Main { private static final int[] DR = {-2, -2, -1, -1, 1, 1, 2, 2}; private static final int[] DC = {-1, 1, -2, 2, -2, 2, -1, 1}; public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner in = new FastScanner(); int testCases = in.nextInt(); int[] queue = new int[300 * 300]; StringBuilder answer = new StringBuilder(); for (int test = 0; test &lt; testCases; test++) { int length = in.nextInt(); int startRow = in.nextInt(); int startCol = in.nextInt(); int targetRow = in.nextInt(); int targetCol = in.nextInt(); int[][] distance = new int[length][length]; for (int row = 0; row &lt; length; row++) { for (int col = 0; col &lt; length; col++) { distance[row][col] = -1; } } int head = 0; int tail = 0; int start = startRow * length + startCol; int target = targetRow * length + targetCol; distance[startRow][startCol] = 0; queue[tail++] = start; while (head &lt; tail &amp;&amp; distance[targetRow][targetCol] == -1) { int square = queue[head++]; int row = square / length; int col = square % length; for (int move = 0; move &lt; 8; move++) { int nextRow = row + DR[move]; int nextCol = col + DC[move]; if (nextRow &lt; 0 || nextRow &gt;= length || nextCol &lt; 0 || nextCol &gt;= length || distance[nextRow][nextCol] != -1) { continue; } distance[nextRow][nextCol] = distance[row][col] + 1; queue[tail++] = nextRow * length + nextCol; } } answer.append(distance[targetRow][targetCol]).append('\n'); } System.out.print(answer); } private static final class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream in = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int pointer; private int length; int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = in.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) { return -1; } } return buffer[pointer++]; } }}

title: LeetCode. 40. Combination Sum II
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Combination Sum II
snippet: LinkApproachSort the candidates, then perform a depth-first search over their indices. Each recursive call chooses only a later index (i + 1), so an array occurrence can be used at most once. Equal values at different indices remain available as separate occurrences.At a given recursion depth, skip a value when it equals the previous candidate at that same depth. This avoids exploring equivalent choices that would produce the same value combination, while still allowing repeated values from different indices to be chosen in a deeper call. Since all candidates are positive and sorted, a candidate larger than the remaining target can end the loop.When the remaining target reaches zero, add a copy of the current path to the result. The copy is important because the path is backtracked and reused after that point.import java.util.ArrayList;import java.util.Arrays;import java.util.List;class Solution { public List&lt;List&lt;Integer&gt;&gt; combinationSum2(int[] candidates, int target) { List&lt;List&lt;Integer&gt;&gt; result = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(); Arrays.sort(candidates); search(candidates, target, 0, new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(), result); return result; } private void search( int[] candidates, int remaining, int start, List&lt;Integer&gt; path, List&lt;List&lt;Integer&gt;&gt; result) { if (remaining == 0) { result.add(new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(path)); return; } for (int i = start; i &lt; candidates.length; i++) { if (i &gt; start &amp;&amp; candidates[i] == candidates[i - 1]) { continue; } if (candidates[i] &gt; remaining) { break; } path.add(candidates[i]); search(candidates, remaining - candidates[i], i + 1, path, result); path.remove(path.size() - 1); } }}The same-depth duplicate check prevents duplicate output combinations; advancing to i + 1 enforces the single-use rule for each occurrence. Sorting takes O(N log N). The search has O(2^N) worst-case time for N candidates, plus the cost of copying each returned combination; the recursion path uses O(N) auxiliary space, excluding output.

title: AtCoder. 020 Log Inequality(3)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Log Inequality
snippet: [Link] https://AtCoder.jp/contests/typical90/tasks/typical90_timport java.util.*;import java.io.*;public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); String[] line = br.readLine().split(" "); long a = atol(line[0]), b = atol(line[1]), c = atol(line[2]); System.out.println(a &lt; pow(c, b) ? "Yes" : "No"); } public static long pow(int base, int exp) { long l = 1; for(int i = 0; i &lt; exp; i++) l *= base; return l; } public static long atol(String s) { return Long.parseLong(s); }}

title: AtCoder. 018 Statue of Chokudai(3)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Statue of Chokudai
snippet: Problem linkLet r = L / 2. At elapsed time E, the wheel has turned through theta = 2π * (E mod T) / T radians, where T is its period. Wrapping the elapsed time by T keeps the angle within one revolution, including when E is greater than T.With the bottom of the wheel at height zero, the passenger’s coordinates in the rotating vertical plane are y = -r sin(theta) and z = r(1 - cos(theta)). The observer is at (X, Y, 0), so the horizontal distance to the passenger is sqrt(X² + (Y - y)²). The elevation angle is atan2(z, horizontal distance); converting that result from radians to degrees gives the required answer. atan2 handles the passenger being at the bottom without a special case.Each query requires a constant number of arithmetic and trigonometric operations, so the time complexity is O(Q). The implementation uses O(Q) space for the output buffer.import java.io.*;public class Main { static class FastScanner { private final InputStream input = System.in; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length; private int pointer; private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = input.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[pointer++]; } long nextLong() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int sign = 1; if (c == '-') { sign = -1; c = read(); } long value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return sign * value; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); long period = input.nextLong(); double radius = input.nextLong() / 2.0; double observerX = input.nextLong(); double observerY = input.nextLong(); int q = (int) input.nextLong(); StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i &lt; q; i++) { long elapsed = input.nextLong(); double theta = 2.0 * Math.PI * (elapsed % period) / period; double passengerY = -radius * Math.sin(theta); double passengerZ = radius * (1.0 - Math.cos(theta)); double horizontal = Math.hypot(observerX, observerY - passengerY); double angle = Math.toDegrees(Math.atan2(passengerZ, horizontal)); output.append(angle).append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); }}

title: AtCoder. 016 Minimum Coins(3)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Minimum Coins
snippet: Problem linkLet dp[x] be the minimum number of coins needed to make total x. Set dp[0] = 0; for every positive amount, the last coin must be one of the three denominations A, B, or C. Therefore,dp[x] = min(dp[x - coin] + 1) over each denomination coin &lt;= x.Process amounts in increasing order so that dp[x - coin] already includes any number of uses of that coin. This is unbounded coin change: each denomination can be used repeatedly. The order of the three input denominations does not matter because every amount considers all three. The target is guaranteed to be reachable by the problem constraints.Use N + 1 as the unreachable sentinel. Any reachable amount can be made with at most N coins because each denomination is a positive integer, so this sentinel is larger than every possible answer. The algorithm takes O(3N) = O(N) time and O(N) space.import java.io.*;public class Main { static class FastScanner { private final InputStream input = System.in; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length = 0; private int pointer = 0; private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = input.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[pointer++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner scanner = new FastScanner(); int target = scanner.nextInt(); int[] coins = { scanner.nextInt(), scanner.nextInt(), scanner.nextInt() }; int unreachable = target + 1; int[] dp = new int[target + 1]; for (int amount = 1; amount &lt;= target; amount++) { dp[amount] = unreachable; for (int coin : coins) { if (coin &lt;= amount &amp;&amp; dp[amount - coin] != unreachable) { dp[amount] = Math.min(dp[amount], dp[amount - coin] + 1); } } } System.out.println(dp[target]); }}

title: AtCoder. 015 Don't be too close(6)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Don't be too close
snippet: Problem linkGiven N positions in a row, for every k from 1 through N, count the ways to choose k positions so that no two chosen positions are adjacent. Print each answer modulo 1,000,000,007.Suppose the chosen positions are x_1 &lt; x_2 &lt; ... &lt; x_k. Since consecutive choices cannot be adjacent, each gap satisfies x_(i+1) &gt;= x_i + 2. Shift the i-th chosen position left by i - 1, defining y_i = x_i - (i - 1). The y_i are now strictly increasing positions chosen from 1 through N - k + 1. This is a bijection: from any k distinct positions in that shortened range, adding i - 1 to the i-th one recovers a unique valid selection in the original row. Therefore the answer is C(N - k + 1, k). If k &gt; N - k + 1, there are not enough positions after removing the required gaps, so the answer is zero.Precompute factorials through N, then compute inverse factorials using Fermat’s little theorem: for nonzero a modulo the prime MOD, a^(MOD-1) ≡ 1, so a^(MOD-2) is its inverse. One binary exponentiation obtains the inverse of N!; walking downward gives every inverse factorial. Then C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!) is evaluated with modular multiplication.The preprocessing takes O(N + log MOD) time and O(N) space; each of the N answers takes constant time. Products of two residues fit in Java long because they are below MOD^2 &lt; Long.MAX_VALUE.import java.io.*;public class Main { static final long MOD = 1_000_000_007L; static class FastScanner { private final InputStream input; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length = 0; private int pointer = 0; FastScanner(InputStream input) { this.input = input; } private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = input.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[pointer++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } } static long modPow(long base, long exponent) { long result = 1; while (exponent &gt; 0) { if ((exponent &amp; 1) == 1) result = result * base % MOD; base = base * base % MOD; exponent &gt;&gt;= 1; } return result; } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(System.in); int n = input.nextInt(); long[] factorial = new long[n + 1]; long[] inverseFactorial = new long[n + 1]; factorial[0] = 1; for (int i = 1; i &lt;= n; i++) { factorial[i] = factorial[i - 1] * i % MOD; } inverseFactorial[n] = modPow(factorial[n], MOD - 2); for (int i = n; i &gt; 0; i--) { inverseFactorial[i - 1] = inverseFactorial[i] * i % MOD; } StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int k = 1; k &lt;= n; k++) { int available = n - k + 1; long ways = 0; if (k &lt;= available) { ways = factorial[available] * inverseFactorial[k] % MOD * inverseFactorial[available - k] % MOD; } output.append(ways).append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); }}

title: AtCoder. 014 We Used to Sing a Song Together(3)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, We Used to Sing a Song Together
snippet: Problem linkGiven two arrays of N integers, pair every value in the first array with one value in the second so that the sum of absolute differences is minimized.Sort both arrays in nondecreasing order and pair elements at the same indices. To see why this is optimal, consider two first-array values x &lt;= y and two second-array values u &lt;= v. Pairing them in the same order costs |x - u| + |y - v|; crossing them costs |x - v| + |y - u|. The same-order cost is never greater: on the number line, matching ordered endpoints avoids the extra distance introduced by crossing. Therefore any crossed pair can be uncrossed without increasing the total, and repeatedly uncrossing yields the sorted, rank-by-rank pairing.The arrays are sorted in O(N log N) time, followed by one linear pass. The total running time is O(N log N) and the arrays use O(N) space. Cast to long before subtracting: two valid int values can have a difference larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE, and the total may also exceed the int range.import java.io.*;import java.util.*;public class Main { static class FastScanner { private final InputStream input; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length = 0; private int pointer = 0; FastScanner(InputStream input) { this.input = input; } private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = input.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[pointer++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int sign = 1; if (c == '-') { sign = -1; c = read(); } int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return sign * value; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(System.in); int n = input.nextInt(); int[] a = new int[n]; int[] b = new int[n]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) a[i] = input.nextInt(); for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) b[i] = input.nextInt(); Arrays.sort(a); Arrays.sort(b); long total = 0; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { total += Math.abs((long) a[i] - b[i]); } System.out.println(total); }}

title: AtCoder. 013 Passing(5)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Graph, Passing, Review, difficult
snippet: Problem linkFor each vertex i, the answer is the shortest distance from vertex 1 to i plus the shortest distance from i to vertex N. The graph is undirected, so the second distance equals the shortest distance from N to i. Run Dijkstra’s algorithm once from vertex 1 and once from vertex N, then add the two distances for every vertex.Store each edge in an adjacency list. Dijkstra’s algorithm is valid because all edge weights are nonnegative; with negative weights, settling the currently closest vertex is not safe. The priority queue may contain outdated entries, so discard an entry when its distance no longer matches the distance array. Keep weights and distances as long. INF marks an unreachable vertex, and the program prints -1 if either search cannot reach a vertex. Before relaxing an edge, it checks that adding the weight stays below INF, avoiding overflow and preserving the unreachable sentinel.Each run takes O((N + M) log N) time with a priority queue and adjacency lists. Running it twice does not change the asymptotic bound. The graph and the two distance arrays use O(N + M) space.import java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;import java.util.ArrayList;import java.util.Arrays;import java.util.List;import java.util.PriorityQueue;public class Main { private static final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4; private static class Edge { final int to; final long weight; Edge(int to, long weight) { this.to = to; this.weight = weight; } } private static class State { final int vertex; final long distance; State(int vertex, long distance) { this.vertex = vertex; this.distance = distance; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int vertexCount = input.nextInt(); int edgeCount = input.nextInt(); List&lt;List&lt;Edge&gt;&gt; graph = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(vertexCount); for (int vertex = 0; vertex &lt; vertexCount; vertex++) { graph.add(new ArrayList&lt;&gt;()); } for (int i = 0; i &lt; edgeCount; i++) { int a = input.nextInt() - 1; int b = input.nextInt() - 1; long weight = input.nextLong(); graph.get(a).add(new Edge(b, weight)); graph.get(b).add(new Edge(a, weight)); } long[] fromStart = dijkstra(graph, 0); long[] fromGoal = dijkstra(graph, vertexCount - 1); StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int vertex = 0; vertex &lt; vertexCount; vertex++) { if (fromStart[vertex] == INF || fromGoal[vertex] == INF) { output.append(-1); } else { output.append(fromStart[vertex] + fromGoal[vertex]); } output.append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); } private static long[] dijkstra(List&lt;List&lt;Edge&gt;&gt; graph, int source) { long[] distance = new long[graph.size()]; Arrays.fill(distance, INF); distance[source] = 0; PriorityQueue&lt;State&gt; queue = new PriorityQueue&lt;&gt;( (left, right) -&gt; Long.compare(left.distance, right.distance)); queue.add(new State(source, 0)); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { State current = queue.poll(); if (current.distance != distance[current.vertex]) { continue; } for (Edge edge : graph.get(current.vertex)) { if (edge.weight &gt;= INF - current.distance) { continue; } long candidate = current.distance + edge.weight; if (candidate &lt; distance[edge.to]) { distance[edge.to] = candidate; queue.add(new State(edge.to, candidate)); } } } return distance; } private static class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int position; private int length; private int read() throws IOException { if (position == length) { length = input.read(buffer); position = 0; if (length == -1) { return -1; } } return buffer[position++]; } private long nextLong() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); long value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } private int nextInt() throws IOException { return (int) nextLong(); } }}

title: AtCoder. 012 Red Painting(4)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Red Painting
snippet: Problem linkInitially, every cell is white. Each operation either paints a cell red or asks whether two cells are connected using only red cells and four-directional moves. Print Yes if both queried cells are red and one can reach the other; otherwise print No.Treat every grid cell as an element of a disjoint-set union (DSU), and keep a separate red array to record which cells have been painted. When a cell is painted for the first time, activate it and unite it with each in-bounds red neighbor. Cells never become white again, so connectivity only merges; the DSU therefore continues to represent the connected components of all red cells.For a query, first require both cells to be red, then compare their DSU representatives. The explicit red check ensures that an unpainted cell is not considered connected even to itself. Neighbor coordinates are checked before accessing the grid.With path compression and union by size, each DSU operation takes amortized O(α(HW)) time. Every cell is activated at most once and has only four neighbors to inspect, so the total time is O((HW + Q) α(HW)). The DSU and red-cell array use O(HW) space.import java.io.*;public class Main { static class FastScanner { private final InputStream input; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length = 0; private int pointer = 0; FastScanner(InputStream input) { this.input = input; } private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = input.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[pointer++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } } static class DSU { private final int[] parent; private final int[] size; DSU(int n) { parent = new int[n]; size = new int[n]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { parent[i] = i; size[i] = 1; } } int find(int x) { if (parent[x] != x) parent[x] = find(parent[x]); return parent[x]; } void unite(int a, int b) { int rootA = find(a); int rootB = find(b); if (rootA == rootB) return; if (size[rootA] &lt; size[rootB]) { int temp = rootA; rootA = rootB; rootB = temp; } parent[rootB] = rootA; size[rootA] += size[rootB]; } } static final int[] DR = {-1, 1, 0, 0}; static final int[] DC = {0, 0, -1, 1}; public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(System.in); int h = input.nextInt(); int w = input.nextInt(); int q = input.nextInt(); int cells = h * w; boolean[] red = new boolean[cells]; DSU dsu = new DSU(cells); StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i &lt; q; i++) { int type = input.nextInt(); if (type == 1) { int r = input.nextInt() - 1; int c = input.nextInt() - 1; int cell = r * w + c; if (!red[cell]) { red[cell] = true; for (int direction = 0; direction &lt; 4; direction++) { int nr = r + DR[direction]; int nc = c + DC[direction]; if (nr &gt;= 0 &amp;&amp; nr &lt; h &amp;&amp; nc &gt;= 0 &amp;&amp; nc &lt; w) { int neighbor = nr * w + nc; if (red[neighbor]) dsu.unite(cell, neighbor); } } } } else { int r1 = input.nextInt() - 1; int c1 = input.nextInt() - 1; int r2 = input.nextInt() - 1; int c2 = input.nextInt() - 1; int first = r1 * w + c1; int second = r2 * w + c2; output.append(red[first] &amp;&amp; red[second] &amp;&amp; dsu.find(first) == dsu.find(second) ? "Yes" : "No").append('\n'); } } System.out.print(output); }}

title: AtCoder. 011 Gravy Jobs(6)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Gravy Jobs, Review, difficult
snippet: Problem linkEach job has a deadline D, duration C, and reward S. Sort the jobs by deadline and process them in that order. Let dp[t] be the maximum reward of a schedule that finishes by time t.For each job, consider taking it by updating dp[t] = max(dp[t], dp[t - C] + S) for t from D down to C. The jobs can be scheduled in deadline order: if two adjacent jobs are out of order, swapping them puts the earlier-deadline job first; its completion only gets earlier, while the second job’s completion time stays the same, so neither deadline is violated. Since deadlines are nondecreasing, all previously processed jobs have deadlines no later than the current one. Appending the current job to any feasible earlier-job schedule that finishes by t - C therefore meets its deadline whenever t &lt;= D. This exchange argument shows that considering jobs in deadline order loses no feasible selection.Iterating t downward ensures dp[t - C] still describes a schedule before the current job was considered, so the same job cannot be selected more than once. After each job, propagate prefix maxima (dp[t] = max(dp[t], dp[t - 1])) so the state means “finishes by time t,” not “uses exactly t time.” The answer is the maximum value in dp. With Dmax the largest deadline, the time complexity is O(N * Dmax) and the space complexity is O(Dmax).import java.io.*;import java.util.*;public class Main { static class FastScanner { private final InputStream input; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length = 0; private int pointer = 0; FastScanner(InputStream input) { this.input = input; } private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = input.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[pointer++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } long nextLong() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); long value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } } static class Job { int deadline; int duration; long reward; Job(int deadline, int duration, long reward) { this.deadline = deadline; this.duration = duration; this.reward = reward; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(System.in); int n = input.nextInt(); Job[] jobs = new Job[n]; int maxDeadline = 0; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { int deadline = input.nextInt(); int duration = input.nextInt(); long reward = input.nextLong(); jobs[i] = new Job(deadline, duration, reward); maxDeadline = Math.max(maxDeadline, deadline); } Arrays.sort(jobs, Comparator.comparingInt(job -&gt; job.deadline)); long[] dp = new long[maxDeadline + 1]; for (Job job : jobs) { for (int time = job.deadline; time &gt;= job.duration; time--) { dp[time] = Math.max(dp[time], dp[time - job.duration] + job.reward); } for (int time = 1; time &lt;= maxDeadline; time++) { dp[time] = Math.max(dp[time], dp[time - 1]); } } long answer = 0; for (long reward : dp) { answer = Math.max(answer, reward); } System.out.println(answer); }}

title: AtCoder. 010 Score Sum Queries(2)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Score Sum Queries
snippet: Problem linkGiven each of N students’ classes and scores, answer queries asking for the total scores of Class 1 and Class 2 in the inclusive range [L, R].Build two prefix-sum arrays, one for each class. classOne[i] stores the Class 1 score total among students 1 through i, and classTwo[i] stores the corresponding Class 2 total. For each student, add the score only to the array for that student’s class; carry the previous prefix value forward in the other array. Thus every student’s score contributes to exactly one class total.Because both ends of the query range are included, subtract the prefix sum through L - 1 from the prefix sum through R. The answer for either class is prefix[R] - prefix[L - 1]. Initializing index zero to zero also handles L = 1 without a special case.Each student is processed once, and each query takes constant time, for O(N + Q) total time. The two prefix arrays use O(N) space. Prefix sums and answers use Java long so large totals do not overflow.import java.io.*;public class Main { static class FastScanner { private final InputStream input; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length = 0; private int pointer = 0; FastScanner(InputStream input) { this.input = input; } private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = input.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[pointer++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int sign = 1; if (c == '-') { sign = -1; c = read(); } int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return sign * value; } long nextLong() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int sign = 1; if (c == '-') { sign = -1; c = read(); } long value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return sign * value; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(System.in); int n = input.nextInt(); long[] classOne = new long[n + 1]; long[] classTwo = new long[n + 1]; for (int i = 1; i &lt;= n; i++) { int classNumber = input.nextInt(); long score = input.nextLong(); classOne[i] = classOne[i - 1]; classTwo[i] = classTwo[i - 1]; if (classNumber == 1) { classOne[i] += score; } else { classTwo[i] += score; } } int q = input.nextInt(); StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i &lt; q; i++) { int left = input.nextInt(); int right = input.nextInt(); long sumOne = classOne[right] - classOne[left - 1]; long sumTwo = classTwo[right] - classTwo[left - 1]; output.append(sumOne).append(' ').append(sumTwo).append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); }}

title: AtCoder. 009 Three Point Angle(6)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Three Point Angle, Review
snippet: Problem linkFor each point as a pivot, consider the directions from it to every other point. Any choice of two such directions forms an angle at the pivot, so the answer is the largest smaller angle among all pairs of directions.After sorting the directions in degrees in [0, 360), duplicate the sorted list with 360 added to each copied angle. For each direction, only the next m - 1 entries are relevant, where m = N - 1; they represent every other direction exactly once, including directions across the 0° boundary. The smaller angle is largest when the two directions are as close as possible to being opposite (180° apart). Therefore, binary-search for angle + 180° in that range and check the lower-bound position and its predecessor. Those are the closest candidates on either side of the ideal opposite direction.For each candidate, let diff be the nonnegative angular difference. The smaller angle is min(diff, 360 - diff). Taking the maximum over all pivots and pairs gives the required angle in degrees. Sorting and searching for each pivot takes O(N log N) time, for O(N² log N) total time. The angle arrays use O(N) working space.import java.io.*;import java.util.*;public class Main { static class FastScanner { private final InputStream input = System.in; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length; private int pointer; private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = input.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[pointer++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int sign = 1; if (c == '-') { sign = -1; c = read(); } int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return sign * value; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner input = new FastScanner(); int n = input.nextInt(); int[] x = new int[n]; int[] y = new int[n]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { x[i] = input.nextInt(); y[i] = input.nextInt(); } int m = n - 1; double answer = 0.0; double[] angles = new double[m]; double[] doubled = new double[2 * m]; for (int pivot = 0; pivot &lt; n; pivot++) { int size = 0; for (int point = 0; point &lt; n; point++) { if (point == pivot) continue; double dx = (double) x[point] - x[pivot]; double dy = (double) y[point] - y[pivot]; double angle = Math.toDegrees(Math.atan2(dy, dx)); if (angle &lt; 0) angle += 360.0; angles[size++] = angle; } Arrays.sort(angles); for (int i = 0; i &lt; m; i++) { doubled[i] = angles[i]; doubled[i + m] = angles[i] + 360.0; } for (int i = 0; i &lt; m; i++) { double target = angles[i] + 180.0; int low = i + 1; int high = i + m; while (low &lt; high) { int middle = low + (high - low) / 2; if (doubled[middle] &lt; target) low = middle + 1; else high = middle; } answer = Math.max(answer, smallerAngle(doubled[low] - angles[i])); if (low &gt; i + 1) { answer = Math.max(answer, smallerAngle(doubled[low - 1] - angles[i])); } } } System.out.println(answer); } static double smallerAngle(double difference) { return Math.min(difference, 360.0 - difference); }}

title: AtCoder. 008 AtCounter(4)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, AtCounter
snippet: Given a string S, count the subsequences equal to atcoder. A subsequence is formed by deleting zero or more characters without changing the order of the remaining characters. Different choices of positions count as different subsequences.Let dp[j] be the number of ways to form the first j characters of atcoder from the characters processed so far. Initially, dp[0] = 1 represents the one way to form the empty prefix, and all other entries are zero. For each input character, visit matching target positions from right to left and add dp[j] into dp[j + 1], modulo 1,000,000,007. The descending order ensures that a character from the current input position cannot be used more than once: the source count still describes subsequences formed before this character was processed.The invariant is that after processing any prefix of S, dp[j] counts exactly the index choices forming the first j target characters within that prefix. The answer is dp[7]. Each input character checks the seven target positions, so the time complexity is O(7N) and the auxiliary space is O(1).Problem linkJavaimport java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;public class Main { private static final long MOD = 1_000_000_007L; private static final String TARGET = "atcoder"; public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { BufferedInputStream in = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); int n = 0; int c; while ((c = in.read()) &lt;= ' ') { if (c == -1) return; } do { n = n * 10 + c - '0'; c = in.read(); } while (c &gt; ' '); char[] s = new char[n]; int length = 0; while (length &lt; n) { c = in.read(); if (c &gt; ' ') s[length++] = (char) c; } long[] dp = new long[TARGET.length() + 1]; dp[0] = 1; for (char ch : s) { for (int j = TARGET.length() - 1; j &gt;= 0; j--) { if (ch == TARGET.charAt(j)) { dp[j + 1] = (dp[j + 1] + dp[j]) % MOD; } } } System.out.println(dp[TARGET.length()]); }}

title: AtCoder. 007 CP Classes(3)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, CP Classes
