title: Programmers — Largest Number
tags: C++, Algorithm, Coding Interview, Programmers, Largest Number, 가장 큰 수, 프로그래머스
snippet: [Link] https://programmers.co.kr/learn/courses/30/lessons/42746ApproachConvert each number to a decimal string, then sort the strings with the rule that a comes before b exactly when a + b &gt; b + a. For example, "3" precedes "30" because "330" &gt; "303". After sorting, concatenating in order produces the largest possible number.This comparator is justified by an exchange argument. For any two neighboring strings a and b in a concatenation, the two possible orders contribute either a + b or b + a; all surrounding digits remain unchanged. Choosing the larger of these two therefore never makes the result worse. Sorting applies this pairwise ordering throughout, so no adjacent exchange can improve the result and the resulting concatenation is maximal.If the first sorted string is "0", every input number is zero, so return "0" rather than a string of repeated zeroes. The solution assumes the input contains at least one non-negative integer, as in the problem constraints.Sorting performs O(N log N) comparisons, each taking O(L) character work for concatenation and comparison, where L is the maximum number of digits in an input number. The final output takes O(NL) time and space.C++#include &lt;algorithm&gt;#include &lt;string&gt;#include &lt;vector&gt;using namespace std;string solution(vector&lt;int&gt; numbers) { vector&lt;string&gt; values; values.reserve(numbers.size()); for (int number : numbers) { values.push_back(to_string(number)); } sort(values.begin(), values.end(), [](const string&amp; a, const string&amp; b) { return a + b &gt; b + a; }); if (values.front() == "0") { return "0"; } string answer; for (const string&amp; value : values) { answer += value; } return answer;}

title: LeetCode. 38. Count and Say
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Count and Say
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/count-and-say/ApproachStart with the first term, "1". To produce each next term, scan the current term from left to right, identify each maximal run of equal digits, and append the run’s length followed by its digit. The scan advances past the entire run, so every digit is encoded exactly once. Repeating this transformation n - 1 times produces the requested term.Let L_k be the length of the term after round k. Processing a term takes time proportional to its length, and appending creates the next term, so total time is O(sum of generated term lengths). The current and next terms are the only strings retained during a round; working space is O(current term length) (the next term is bounded by a constant factor of the current term length).Javaclass Solution { public String countAndSay(int n) { String term = "1"; for (int round = 1; round &lt; n; round++) { StringBuilder next = new StringBuilder(); int i = 0; while (i &lt; term.length()) { char digit = term.charAt(i); int end = i + 1; while (end &lt; term.length() &amp;&amp; term.charAt(end) == digit) { end++; } next.append(end - i).append(digit); i = end; } term = next.toString(); } return term; }}

title: BOJ. Tomato (7569)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Heap, Coding Interview, BOJ, Tomato, 토마토
snippet: Problem linkEach tomato box is a three-dimensional grid. A ripe tomato ripens its unripe neighbors in the six axis-aligned directions, and all changes happen simultaneously one day at a time. The task is to find the number of days until no unripe tomatoes remain, or report -1 if some can never ripen.Use multi-source breadth-first search: enqueue every initially ripe tomato before searching. Store each queued cell as one flattened integer index in a primitive int[] whose capacity is the total number of cells. A cell is enqueued only when it changes from unripe to ripe, so it enters the queue at most once.The grid value doubles as the day label: initial ripe cells are 1, and a newly ripened cell gets its predecessor’s value plus one. Thus each BFS layer represents one simultaneous day. Count unripe cells while reading input; decrement the count as they ripen. If it starts at zero, the answer is 0. If it is still positive after the queue is exhausted, return -1; otherwise the largest grid value minus one is the number of elapsed days.The input reader parses whitespace-separated integers without relying on line boundaries.import java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;public class Main { private static int m, n, h; private static final int[] DZ = {1, -1, 0, 0, 0, 0}; private static final int[] DY = {0, 0, 1, -1, 0, 0}; private static final int[] DX = {0, 0, 0, 0, 1, -1}; public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner in = new FastScanner(); m = in.nextInt(); n = in.nextInt(); h = in.nextInt(); int volume = m * n * h; int[][][] box = new int[h][n][m]; int[] queue = new int[volume]; int tail = 0; int unripe = 0; for (int z = 0; z &lt; h; z++) { for (int y = 0; y &lt; n; y++) { for (int x = 0; x &lt; m; x++) { int value = in.nextInt(); box[z][y][x] = value; if (value == 1) { queue[tail++] = (z * n + y) * m + x; } else if (value == 0) { unripe++; } } } } System.out.println(ripeningDays(box, queue, tail, unripe)); } private static int ripeningDays(int[][][] box, int[] queue, int tail, int unripe) { if (unripe == 0) { return 0; } int maxDay = 1; for (int head = 0; head &lt; tail; head++) { int index = queue[head]; int z = index / (n * m); int remainder = index % (n * m); int y = remainder / m; int x = remainder % m; int nextDay = box[z][y][x] + 1; for (int direction = 0; direction &lt; 6; direction++) { int nz = z + DZ[direction]; int ny = y + DY[direction]; int nx = x + DX[direction]; if (nz &lt; 0 || nz &gt;= h || ny &lt; 0 || ny &gt;= n || nx &lt; 0 || nx &gt;= m || box[nz][ny][nx] != 0) { continue; } box[nz][ny][nx] = nextDay; maxDay = nextDay; unripe--; queue[tail++] = (nz * n + ny) * m + nx; } } return unripe == 0 ? maxDay - 1 : -1; } private static final class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream in = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int pointer, length; int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } private int read() throws IOException { if (pointer == length) { length = in.read(buffer); pointer = 0; if (length == -1) { return -1; } } return buffer[pointer++]; } }}Every cell is inserted at most once and checks at most six neighbors, so the running time is O(MNH). The grid and primitive queue each use O(MNH) storage.

title: LeetCode. 37. Sudoku Solver
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Sudoku Solver
snippet: A valid Sudoku board has one solution. Fill the empty cells in place so that every row, column, and 3 × 3 box contains each digit from 1 to 9 exactly once.Problem linkApproachFor each row, column, and box, a 9-bit mask records which digits are already present. Bit d represents digit d + 1; a set bit means that digit cannot be placed there. Thus the legal digits for an empty cell are the bits in the full mask that are absent from all three corresponding masks.At each recursive step, scan the remaining empty cells and choose the one with the fewest legal digits (minimum remaining values, or MRV). This constraint-first choice reduces the branching factor early. If a cell has no legal digit, the current branch is impossible. Otherwise, try each candidate: write it into the board and set its three mask bits, then recurse. A failed branch clears those bits and restores '.'; a successful branch returns immediately, leaving the completed solution in the input board.For up to 81 cells, the worst-case search is exponential (at most nine choices per empty cell), while MRV makes the search practical by exposing contradictions early and narrowing branching. The auxiliary space is O(81) for the recursion and fixed-size masks; the board is modified in place.Javaclass Solution { private static final int FULL = (1 &lt;&lt; 9) - 1; private char[][] board; private final int[] rows = new int[9]; private final int[] columns = new int[9]; private final int[] boxes = new int[9]; public void solveSudoku(char[][] board) { for (int i = 0; i &lt; 9; i++) { rows[i] = 0; columns[i] = 0; boxes[i] = 0; } this.board = board; for (int row = 0; row &lt; 9; row++) { for (int column = 0; column &lt; 9; column++) { char cell = board[row][column]; if (cell != '.') { int bit = 1 &lt;&lt; (cell - '1'); int box = (row / 3) * 3 + column / 3; rows[row] |= bit; columns[column] |= bit; boxes[box] |= bit; } } } solve(); } private boolean solve() { int bestRow = -1; int bestColumn = -1; int bestCandidates = 0; int fewestChoices = 10; for (int row = 0; row &lt; 9; row++) { for (int column = 0; column &lt; 9; column++) { if (board[row][column] != '.') { continue; } int box = (row / 3) * 3 + column / 3; int candidates = FULL &amp; ~(rows[row] | columns[column] | boxes[box]); int choices = Integer.bitCount(candidates); if (choices &lt; fewestChoices) { bestRow = row; bestColumn = column; bestCandidates = candidates; fewestChoices = choices; if (choices &lt;= 1) { break; } } } if (fewestChoices &lt;= 1) { break; } } if (bestRow == -1) { return true; } if (bestCandidates == 0) { return false; } int box = (bestRow / 3) * 3 + bestColumn / 3; while (bestCandidates != 0) { int bit = bestCandidates &amp; -bestCandidates; bestCandidates -= bit; int digit = Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros(bit); board[bestRow][bestColumn] = (char) ('1' + digit); rows[bestRow] |= bit; columns[bestColumn] |= bit; boxes[box] |= bit; if (solve()) { return true; } rows[bestRow] &amp;= ~bit; columns[bestColumn] &amp;= ~bit; boxes[box] &amp;= ~bit; board[bestRow][bestColumn] = '.'; } return false; }}

title: LeetCode. 36. Valid Sudoku
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Valid Sudoku
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-sudoku/The board is valid when no filled digit is repeated in any row, column, or 3×3 box. Empty cells (.) are ignored; the partially filled board does not need to be solvable.Keep one bitmask for each row, column, and box. A digit d maps to 1 &lt;&lt; (d - '1'), and the box index for cell (r, c) is (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3. If the bit is already set in any of those three masks, the digit is a duplicate. Otherwise, set it in all three masks.Each of the 81 cells is processed once, so the time complexity is O(81). The fixed arrays use constant additional space, O(1).class Solution { public boolean isValidSudoku(char[][] board) { int[] rows = new int[9]; int[] columns = new int[9]; int[] boxes = new int[9]; for (int r = 0; r &lt; 9; r++) { for (int c = 0; c &lt; 9; c++) { char value = board[r][c]; if (value == '.') { continue; } int bit = 1 &lt;&lt; (value - '1'); int box = (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3; if ((rows[r] &amp; bit) != 0 || (columns[c] &amp; bit) != 0 || (boxes[box] &amp; bit) != 0) { return false; } rows[r] |= bit; columns[c] |= bit; boxes[box] |= bit; } } return true; }}

title: BOJ. Tell Median Value (1655)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Heap, Coding Interview, BOJ, Maximum heap, 가운데를 말해요
snippet: BOJ 1655: Say the Middle NumberMaintain the values seen so far in two priority queues. lower is a max-heap containing the lower half, and upper is a min-heap containing the upper half. Keep both invariants: Every value in lower is less than or equal to every value in upper. lower has either the same number of values as upper, or exactly one more.For each input value, insert it into the heap whose range it belongs to, then move a root to the other heap if needed to restore the size invariant. The root of lower is then the lower median. When the prefix length is odd, lower has one extra value and its root is the middle element. When the prefix length is even, the two heaps have equal size, and the root of lower is the smaller of the two central values, as required by the problem.The heaps contain all input values exactly once, so space usage is O(N). Each insertion and possible rebalancing move takes O(log N), giving O(N log N) time overall. Input is read as whitespace-separated integers using a buffered byte reader.import java.io.BufferedInputStream;import java.io.IOException;import java.util.Collections;import java.util.PriorityQueue;public class Main { private static final class FastScanner { private final BufferedInputStream input = new BufferedInputStream(System.in); private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int length = 0; private int position = 0; private int read() throws IOException { if (position == length) { length = input.read(buffer); position = 0; if (length == -1) return -1; } return buffer[position++]; } int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int sign = 1; if (c == '-') { sign = -1; c = read(); } int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value * sign; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner scanner = new FastScanner(); int n = scanner.nextInt(); PriorityQueue&lt;Integer&gt; lower = new PriorityQueue&lt;&gt;(Collections.reverseOrder()); PriorityQueue&lt;Integer&gt; upper = new PriorityQueue&lt;&gt;(); StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { int value = scanner.nextInt(); if (lower.isEmpty() || value &lt;= lower.peek()) { lower.add(value); } else { upper.add(value); } if (lower.size() &gt; upper.size() + 1) { upper.add(lower.poll()); } else if (upper.size() &gt; lower.size()) { lower.add(upper.poll()); } output.append(lower.peek()).append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); }}

title: LeetCode. 34. Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, Binary Search, LeetCode, Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/find-first-and-last-position-of-element-in-sorted-array/Because the array is sorted, two binary searches can find the boundaries. The first search finds the first index whose value is at least target; the second finds the first index whose value is greater than target. If the first boundary is at the end of the array or does not contain target, the target is absent. Otherwise, the answer is the first boundary and one less than the second boundary. Searching for a value greater than target directly avoids computing target + 1, which could overflow for Integer.MAX_VALUE.The loop invariant is that the boundary being sought remains in the half-open interval [left, right). Each iteration discards at least half of the remaining indices, so both searches take O(log N) time. They use O(1) extra space.class Solution { public int[] searchRange(int[] nums, int target) { int left = lowerBound(nums, target); if (left == nums.length || nums[left] != target) { return new int[] {-1, -1}; } int right = upperBound(nums, target); return new int[] {left, right - 1}; } private int lowerBound(int[] nums, int target) { int left = 0, right = nums.length; while (left &lt; right) { int mid = left + (right - left) / 2; if (nums[mid] &lt; target) { left = mid + 1; } else { right = mid; } } return left; } private int upperBound(int[] nums, int target) { int left = 0, right = nums.length; while (left &lt; right) { int mid = left + (right - left) / 2; if (nums[mid] &lt;= target) { left = mid + 1; } else { right = mid; } } return left; }}

title: LeetCode. 33. Search in Rotated Sorted Array
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, Binary Search, LeetCode, Search in Rotated Sorted Array
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/search-in-rotated-sorted-array/ApproachThe array was sorted in ascending order and then rotated, and all values are distinct. At every binary-search step, at least one half of the current interval is sorted. Check whether the target lies within that half’s inclusive value range; if it does, discard the other half, otherwise discard the sorted half. This keeps the target, if present, in the remaining interval. The loop ends when the interval is empty, which also handles an empty input.The time complexity is O(log N) and the extra space complexity is O(1).Javaclass Solution { public int search(int[] nums, int target) { int left = 0; int right = nums.length - 1; while (left &lt;= right) { int mid = left + (right - left) / 2; if (nums[mid] == target) { return mid; } if (nums[left] &lt;= nums[mid]) { // The left half is sorted. if (nums[left] &lt;= target &amp;&amp; target &lt; nums[mid]) { right = mid - 1; } else { left = mid + 1; } } else { // The right half is sorted. if (nums[mid] &lt; target &amp;&amp; target &lt;= nums[right]) { left = mid + 1; } else { right = mid - 1; } } } return -1; }}

title: LeetCode. 32. Longest Valid Parentheses
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Longest Valid Parentheses, Review, difficult
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-valid-parentheses/ApproachScan the string from left to right while storing character indices in an ArrayDeque&lt;Integer&gt;. The stack starts with the sentinel index -1, which acts as the boundary immediately before the current valid substring.For each opening parenthesis, push its index. For each closing parenthesis, pop the most recent unmatched opening position (or the sentinel). If the stack becomes empty, the closing parenthesis has no matching opening parenthesis, so push its index as the new invalid boundary. Otherwise, the stack top is the index immediately before the valid suffix ending at the current position; its length is i - stack.peek(), so update the maximum.The stack invariant is that, after each character is processed, its top is the boundary before the longest valid suffix ending at the current index, or the latest unmatched closing parenthesis if no such suffix exists. Opening indices below the top delimit unmatched opens; popping one on a close either reveals the boundary for a valid suffix or exposes that the current close is unmatched. The -1 sentinel handles a valid substring beginning at index zero without a separate case.Each index is pushed and popped at most once. The time complexity is O(N) and the auxiliary space complexity is O(N), where N is the string length.Javaimport java.util.ArrayDeque;class Solution { public int longestValidParentheses(String s) { ArrayDeque&lt;Integer&gt; stack = new ArrayDeque&lt;&gt;(); stack.push(-1); int max = 0; for (int i = 0; i &lt; s.length(); i++) { if (s.charAt(i) == '(') { stack.push(i); } else { stack.pop(); if (stack.isEmpty()) { stack.push(i); } else { max = Math.max(max, i - stack.peek()); } } } return max; }}

title: BOJ. Maximum heap (11279)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Heap, Coding Interview, BOJ, Maximum heap, 최대 힙
snippet: [Link] https://www.acmicpc.net/problem/11279A max-heap keeps every parent value greater than or equal to its children, so the largest value is always at the root. Inserting a value appends it at the end and sifts it upward while it is larger than its parent. Removing the maximum replaces the root with the last value and sifts that value downward by swapping with the larger child. Each operation follows at most one root-to-leaf path, so insertion and removal take O(log N) time. The primitive array uses O(N) space; its capacity is enough for the maximum possible number of insert commands.The input is read as whitespace-separated tokens, and all results are accumulated in a StringBuilder. A removal from an empty heap prints 0, as required.import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.IOException;import java.io.InputStreamReader;import java.util.StringTokenizer;public class Main { private static BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); private static StringTokenizer tokenizer; private static int nextInt() throws IOException { while (tokenizer == null || !tokenizer.hasMoreTokens()) { tokenizer = new StringTokenizer(reader.readLine()); } return Integer.parseInt(tokenizer.nextToken()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { int n = nextInt(); int[] heap = new int[n + 1]; int size = 0; StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { int value = nextInt(); if (value == 0) { if (size == 0) { output.append(0).append('\n'); } else { output.append(heap[1]).append('\n'); heap[1] = heap[size--]; int parent = 1; while (parent * 2 &lt;= size) { int child = parent * 2; if (child + 1 &lt;= size &amp;&amp; heap[child + 1] &gt; heap[child]) { child++; } if (heap[parent] &gt;= heap[child]) { break; } int temp = heap[parent]; heap[parent] = heap[child]; heap[child] = temp; parent = child; } } } else { int child = ++size; while (child &gt; 1 &amp;&amp; heap[child / 2] &lt; value) { heap[child] = heap[child / 2]; child /= 2; } heap[child] = value; } } System.out.print(output); }}

title: Codility. ArrayInversionCount
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, Codility, ArrayInversionCount
snippet: The inversion count of an array is the number of pairs of indices i &lt; j for which A[i] &gt; A[j]. Equal values do not form an inversion. Inserting each value into a sorted ArrayList uses binary search to find a position, but shifting elements still takes O(N) per insertion, for O(N²) total time.Merge sort counts inversions in O(N log N). Recursively sort each half, then merge the halves into one sorted range. At every step of the merge, both unmerged portions are sorted. If the next right-side value is smaller than the next left-side value, it is smaller than every remaining value on the left, so all of those left-side values form inversions with it. Add their count and take the right value. Otherwise take the left value; choosing the left value on equality ensures equal elements are not counted. A single auxiliary array is reused throughout the recursion.The count is accumulated as a long to avoid overflow and the method returns -1 only when the total exceeds 1,000,000,000. Empty and one-element arrays have no pairs, so the method returns 0. The running time is O(N log N) and the auxiliary space is O(N) (with O(log N) recursion depth).class Solution { private static final long LIMIT = 1_000_000_000L; public int solution(int[] A) { if (A.length &lt; 2) { return 0; } int[] auxiliary = new int[A.length]; long inversions = sortAndCount(A, auxiliary, 0, A.length); return inversions &gt; LIMIT ? -1 : (int) inversions; } // Sorts the half-open range [start, end) and returns its inversion count. private long sortAndCount(int[] values, int[] auxiliary, int start, int end) { if (end - start &lt; 2) { return 0; } int middle = start + (end - start) / 2; long inversions = sortAndCount(values, auxiliary, start, middle) + sortAndCount(values, auxiliary, middle, end); int left = start; int right = middle; int output = start; while (left &lt; middle &amp;&amp; right &lt; end) { if (values[left] &lt;= values[right]) { auxiliary[output++] = values[left++]; } else { auxiliary[output++] = values[right++]; inversions += middle - left; } } while (left &lt; middle) { auxiliary[output++] = values[left++]; } while (right &lt; end) { auxiliary[output++] = values[right++]; } System.arraycopy(auxiliary, start, values, start, end - start); return inversions; }}[Link] https://app.codility.com/programmers/trainings/4/array_inversion_count/

title: LeetCode. 35. Search Insert Position
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Search Insert Position
snippet: ProblemApproachUse binary search to find the lower bound: the first index whose value is greater than or equal to target. Maintain a half-open search interval [left, right). At the start, it contains every valid array index. At each step, left is a boundary before which every value is less than target, while right is a boundary at or after which every value is at least target. If the midpoint value is less than target, move left past it; otherwise, move right to the midpoint. The interval shrinks until left == right, which is the lower-bound index. If every value is smaller, that index is nums.length; an empty array naturally returns zero. Choosing the first value that is at least the target also handles duplicates.The search takes O(log N) time and O(1) auxiliary space.Javaclass Solution { public int searchInsert(int[] nums, int target) { int left = 0; int right = nums.length; while (left &lt; right) { int mid = left + (right - left) / 2; if (nums[mid] &lt; target) { left = mid + 1; } else { right = mid; } } return left; }}

title: LeetCode. 31. Next Permutation
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Next Permutation
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/next-permutation/ApproachTo obtain the smallest permutation that is still greater than the current one, change the rightmost position that can be increased. Scan from right to left for the first index i where nums[i] &lt; nums[i + 1]. The suffix after i is nonincreasing; if no such index exists, the entire array is nonincreasing and is already the greatest permutation, so reverse it to get the smallest order.When a pivot exists, find the rightmost suffix value greater than nums[i] and swap them. The suffix’s nonincreasing order means this rightmost greater value is the smallest value that can replace the pivot while making the whole number larger. Reverse the suffix to put its values in increasing order, producing the smallest possible remainder.The algorithm runs in O(N) time and uses O(1) extra space.Javaclass Solution { public void nextPermutation(int[] nums) { int pivot = nums.length - 2; while (pivot &gt;= 0 &amp;&amp; nums[pivot] &gt;= nums[pivot + 1]) { pivot--; } if (pivot &gt;= 0) { int successor = nums.length - 1; while (nums[successor] &lt;= nums[pivot]) { successor--; } swap(nums, pivot, successor); } reverse(nums, pivot + 1, nums.length - 1); } private void reverse(int[] nums, int left, int right) { while (left &lt; right) { swap(nums, left++, right--); } } private void swap(int[] nums, int left, int right) { int temp = nums[left]; nums[left] = nums[right]; nums[right] = temp; }}

title: LeetCode. 30. Substring with Concatenation of All Words
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Substring with Concatenation of All Words
snippet: LinkApproachAll words have the same nonzero length, so we can scan aligned word-sized chunks with sliding windows. Process each starting offset from 0 through wordLength - 1. The target map stores the required frequency of each word, while window stores its frequency in the current window; this handles duplicate words as well as unique ones.When the right side encounters a word absent from target, no valid concatenation can cross it: clear the window and move the left pointer to the position after that word. Otherwise, add the word and shrink from the left while its frequency exceeds the target frequency. When the window contains exactly words.length words, record its starting index, then remove its leftmost word. Shrinking once after a match preserves the possibility of finding overlapping matches. Since offsets are scanned separately, sort the collected indices before returning them.Let N be the length of s, L the common word length, W the number of words, U the number of distinct words, and R the number of returned indices. Across all offsets, the right pointer processes O(N) word chunks. Extracting each chunk costs O(L), and sorting the results costs O(R log R), for a total time of O(N * L + R log R). The frequency maps and active window use O(U + W) space; the returned output uses an additional O(R).Javaclass Solution { public List&lt;Integer&gt; findSubstring(String s, String[] words) { List&lt;Integer&gt; result = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(); if (words.length == 0) { return result; } int wordLength = words[0].length(); int wordCount = words.length; int totalLength = wordLength * wordCount; if (s.length() &lt; totalLength) { return result; } Map&lt;String, Integer&gt; target = new HashMap&lt;&gt;(); for (String word : words) { target.put(word, target.getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1); } for (int offset = 0; offset &lt; wordLength; offset++) { Map&lt;String, Integer&gt; window = new HashMap&lt;&gt;(); int left = offset; int right = offset; int count = 0; while (right + wordLength &lt;= s.length()) { String word = s.substring(right, right + wordLength); right += wordLength; if (!target.containsKey(word)) { window.clear(); count = 0; left = right; continue; } window.put(word, window.getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1); count++; while (window.get(word) &gt; target.get(word)) { String removed = s.substring(left, left + wordLength); window.put(removed, window.get(removed) - 1); left += wordLength; count--; } if (count == wordCount) { result.add(left); String removed = s.substring(left, left + wordLength); window.put(removed, window.get(removed) - 1); left += wordLength; count--; } } } Collections.sort(result); return result; }}

title: LeetCode. 29. Divide Two Integers
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Divide Two Integers
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/divide-two-integers/This problem asks us to divide two integers without using multiplication, division, or the remainder operator. The quotient is truncated toward zero. The divisor is guaranteed to be nonzero by the problem constraints.Convert both operands to positive long magnitudes. Casting before taking the absolute value is essential: the positive magnitude of Integer.MIN_VALUE does not fit in an int, but it does fit in a long.Then inspect quotient bits from 31 down to 0. At each bit, compare the remaining dividend with the divisor magnitude shifted left by that bit. If the shifted value fits, subtract it and set that quotient bit. This greedily takes the largest available power-of-two multiple at each step; after all 32 bits, the remainder is smaller than the divisor and the accumulated bits form the quotient magnitude.Apply the sign after constructing the magnitude. The only mathematical quotient outside the int range is Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1, whose positive result is saturated to Integer.MAX_VALUE.The loop always examines 32 bits, so the time complexity is O(32) (equivalently O(1) for fixed-width integers), with O(1) extra space.class Solution { public int divide(int dividend, int divisor) { long dividendMagnitude = Math.abs((long) dividend); long divisorMagnitude = Math.abs((long) divisor); long quotientMagnitude = 0; for (int bit = 31; bit &gt;= 0; bit--) { long shiftedDivisor = divisorMagnitude &lt;&lt; bit; if (shiftedDivisor &lt;= dividendMagnitude) { dividendMagnitude -= shiftedDivisor; quotientMagnitude |= 1L &lt;&lt; bit; } } boolean negative = (dividend &lt; 0) != (divisor &lt; 0); long quotient = negative ? -quotientMagnitude : quotientMagnitude; if (quotient &gt; Integer.MAX_VALUE) { return Integer.MAX_VALUE; } return (int) quotient; }}

title: Programmers. Stock Price
tags: Java, Algorithm, Stack, Coding Interview, Programmers, Stock Price, 주식 가격, 프로그래머스
snippet: [Link] https://programmers.co.kr/learn/courses/30/lessons/42584?language=javaimport java.util.*;class Solution { public int[] solution(int[] prices) { int[] answer = new int[prices.length]; int polledIdx = 0, curIdx; Stack&lt;Integer&gt; stack = new Stack&lt;&gt;(); for(curIdx = 0; curIdx &lt; prices.length; curIdx++) { int price = prices[curIdx]; while(!stack.isEmpty() &amp;&amp; prices[stack.peek()] &gt; price) { int idx = stack.pop(); answer[idx] = curIdx - idx; } stack.add(curIdx); } curIdx--; while(!stack.isEmpty()) { int idx = stack.pop(); answer[idx] = curIdx - idx; } return answer; }}

title: Programmers. Disk Controller
tags: Java, Algorithm, PriorityQueue, Coding Interview, Programmers, Disk Controller, 디스크 컨트롤러, 프로그래머스
snippet: [Link] https://programmers.co.kr/learn/courses/30/lessons/42627?language=java#import java.util.Arrays;import java.util.PriorityQueue;class Solution { public int solution(int[][] jobs) { Arrays.sort(jobs, (l, r) -&gt; l[0] - r[0]); int endT = 0, jobIdx = 0, sum = 0, len = jobs.length; PriorityQueue&lt;int[]&gt; pq = new PriorityQueue&lt;int[]&gt;((l,r)-&gt;l[1]-r[1]); while(jobIdx &lt; len) { while(jobIdx &lt; len &amp;&amp; endT &gt;= jobs[jobIdx][0]) pq.add(jobs[jobIdx++]); if(pq.size() == 0) endT = jobs[jobIdx][0]; else { int[] timeInfo = pq.poll(); endT = endT + timeInfo[1]; sum += endT - timeInfo[0]; } } while(pq.size() != 0) { int[] timeInfo = pq.poll(); endT = endT + timeInfo[1]; sum += endT - timeInfo[0]; } return sum / len; }}

title: BOJ. Closest two Point (2261)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Stack, Coding Interview, BOJ, Closest two Point, Review, difficult
snippet: [Link] https://www.acmicpc.net/problem/2261import java.util.*;import java.util.stream.Stream;import java.io.*;public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); int[] line; int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); Point[] p = new Point[n]; for(int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { line = getLine(br); p[i] = new Point(line[0], line[1]); } Arrays.sort(p, (l,r) -&gt; l.x - r.x); System.out.print(binSearch(p, 0, n - 1, Integer.MAX_VALUE)); } private static int binSearch(Point[] p, int start, int end, int min) { // (2 -&gt; 3Points) Under 3 Points(3 points -&gt; 1 , 2 -&gt; 1 is not searched) if(end - start &lt;= 2) { for(int i = start; i &lt;= end; i++) { for(int j = i + 1; j &lt;= end; j++) { int dis = dis(p[i], p[j]); if(dis &lt; min) min = dis; } } return min; } int mid = (start + end) / 2; int tempMin = Math.min(binSearch(p, start, mid, min), binSearch(p, mid + 1, end, min)); min = Math.min(min, tempMin); return Math.min(midSearch(p, start, end, tempMin), min); } private static int midSearch(Point[] p, int start, int end, int lrMin) { ArrayList&lt;Point&gt; al = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(); int min = Integer.MAX_VALUE, mid = (start + end) / 2; for(int i = start; i &lt;= end; i++) { int xDiff = p[i].x - p[mid].x; if(xDiff * xDiff &lt; lrMin) al.add(p[i]); } al.sort((l, r) -&gt; l.y - r.y); for(int i = 0; i &lt; al.size(); i++) { Point lowP = al.get(i); for(int j = i + 1; j &lt; al.size(); j++) { int yDiff = al.get(j).y - lowP.y; if(yDiff * yDiff &lt; lrMin) { int dis = dis(lowP, al.get(j)); if(dis &lt; min) min = dis; } else break; } } return min; } private static int dis(Point p1, Point p2) { return (p1.x - p2.x) * (p1.x - p2.x) + (p1.y - p2.y) * (p1.y - p2.y); } public static class Point { int x; int y; Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } } private static int[] getLine (BufferedReader br) throws IOException { return Stream.of(br.readLine().split(" ")).mapToInt(Integer::parseInt).toArray(); }}

title: LeetCode. 28. Implement strStr()
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Implement strStr()
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/implement-strstr/The prefix-function (also called the LPS array, for “longest proper prefix which is also a suffix”) records, for every position in needle, the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix ending there. A proper prefix is shorter than the whole string.While building this array, if the next characters do not match, we fall back to the LPS value of the already matched prefix. That value is the longest shorter prefix that could still match, so previously checked characters do not need to be revisited. The same invariant drives the search: j is the length of the needle prefix matching the suffix ending just before i; after a mismatch, j = lps[j - 1] retains the longest viable overlapping prefix instead of restarting from the beginning.An empty needle matches at index 0. Otherwise, the scan returns immediately when all of needle has matched; if the scan ends first, there is no match. The prefix array uses $O(M)$ space, and both its construction and the scan take linear time, for $O(N + M)$ total time, where $N$ and $M$ are the lengths of haystack and needle.class Solution { public int strStr(String haystack, String needle) { int n = haystack.length(); int m = needle.length(); if (m == 0) return 0; int[] lps = new int[m]; for (int i = 1, prefixLength = 0; i &lt; m; ) { if (needle.charAt(i) == needle.charAt(prefixLength)) { lps[i++] = ++prefixLength; } else if (prefixLength &gt; 0) { prefixLength = lps[prefixLength - 1]; } else { lps[i++] = 0; } } // Invariant: j is the longest needle prefix matching a suffix before i. for (int i = 0, j = 0; i &lt; n; ) { if (haystack.charAt(i) == needle.charAt(j)) { i++; j++; if (j == m) return i - m; } else if (j &gt; 0) { // Keep the longest overlapping prefix that can still match. j = lps[j - 1]; } else { i++; } } return -1; }}

title: LeetCode. 27. Remove Element
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Remove Element
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-element/ApproachScan nums from left to right and keep a write index for the next value that should remain. When the current value is not val, copy it to nums[write] and advance write. Values equal to val are skipped.Before each element is processed, the first write positions contain exactly the values unequal to val encountered so far, in their original order. Copying a retained value to the write position cannot disturb any unread element because write never exceeds the current scan position. When the scan finishes, write is the new length and the prefix nums[0..write) is the stable filtered result. The suffix is unspecified and must not be relied on.The method takes O(N) time and O(1) extra space.Javaclass Solution { public int removeElement(int[] nums, int val) { int write = 0; for (int value : nums) { if (value != val) { nums[write++] = value; } } return write; }}

title: LeetCode. 26. Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array/ApproachBecause the input is sorted, equal values are adjacent. Scan the array from left to right with a read index, and keep a write index for the next position where a new distinct value belongs. When the current value differs from the last value written, copy it to the write position and advance the write index.Before each read, the prefix nums[0..write) contains exactly the distinct values from the already processed input, in sorted order. The first value is always written when present; each later value is written only when it differs from the previous distinct value. Thus, an empty array is safe and returns 0; otherwise the method returns the number of distinct values. The resulting distinct values occupy the prefix of the input array, and anything after that prefix can be ignored.The algorithm takes O(N) time and O(1) extra space.Javaclass Solution { public int removeDuplicates(int[] nums) { int write = 0; for (int read = 0; read &lt; nums.length; read++) { if (write == 0 || nums[read] != nums[write - 1]) { nums[write++] = nums[read]; } } return write; }}

title: BOJ. Bigest square in histogram (6549)
tags: Java, Algorithm, Stack, Coding Interview, BOJ, Bigest square in histogram
snippet: [Link] https://www.acmicpc.net/problem/6549import java.util.*;import java.io.*;public class Main{ public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException{ BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); String[] line; int n, w = 0; long max = 0; Stack&lt;Integer&gt; stack = new Stack&lt;&gt;(); StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); while(true) { max = 0; line = br.readLine().split(" "); n = atoi(line[0]); long[] ha = new long[line.length - 1]; for(int i = 0; i &lt; ha.length; i++) ha[i] = atol(line[i + 1]); int i = 0; if(n == 0) break; stack.clear(); while(i &lt; n) { long h = ha[i]; if(!stack.isEmpty()) { if(ha[stack.peek()] &lt;= h) { stack.push(i++); } else { while(!stack.isEmpty() &amp;&amp; ha[stack.peek()] &gt;= h) { long height = ha[stack.pop()], width = stack.isEmpty() ? i : i - 1 - stack.peek(); max = Math.max(max, height * width); } stack.push(i++); } } else { stack.push(i++); } } i = n; while(!stack.isEmpty()) { long height = ha[stack.pop()], width = stack.isEmpty() ? n : n - 1 - stack.peek(); max = Math.max(max, height * width); } sb.append(max + "\n"); } System.out.println(sb); } public static int atoi(String s) { return Integer.parseInt(s); } public static long atol(String s) { return Long.parseLong(s); }}

title: LeetCode. 25. Reverse Nodes in k-Group
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, List, Reverse Nodes in k-Group
snippet: ProblemApproachProcess the list one group at a time. Starting at the first node of a group, walk k - 1 links to find its kth node. If there are fewer than k nodes left, stop: that suffix must remain in its original order. Otherwise, save the node after the group as groupNext, then reverse the group’s links toward groupNext. Initializing the reversed group’s previous pointer to groupNext makes the old first node point to the untouched suffix when the reversal finishes.The kth node becomes the group’s new head, and the old first node becomes its tail. Connect the previous group’s tail to the new head (or set the overall head for the first group), then continue from the old first node, now the tail. This reuses every input node; it does not allocate replacement list nodes.For N nodes, each node is visited a constant number of times, so the time complexity is O(N). The algorithm uses O(1) auxiliary space.Java/** * Definition for singly-linked list. * public class ListNode { * int val; * ListNode next; * ListNode() {} * ListNode(int val) { this.val = val; } * ListNode(int val, ListNode next) { this.val = val; this.next = next; } * } */class Solution { public ListNode reverseKGroup(ListNode head, int k) { ListNode groupPrevious = null; ListNode groupStart = head; while (groupStart != null) { ListNode kth = groupStart; for (int i = 1; i &lt; k &amp;&amp; kth != null; i++) { kth = kth.next; } if (kth == null) { break; } ListNode groupNext = kth.next; ListNode previous = groupNext; ListNode current = groupStart; while (current != groupNext) { ListNode next = current.next; current.next = previous; previous = current; current = next; } if (groupPrevious == null) { head = kth; } else { groupPrevious.next = kth; } groupPrevious = groupStart; groupStart = groupNext; } return head; }}

title: LeetCode. 24. Swap Nodes in Pairs
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, List, Swap Nodes in Pairs, Review, difficult
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/swap-nodes-in-pairs/Swap each adjacent pair by relinking its next references; the values are never changed, and every input node is reused.A dummy head gives the first pair a predecessor, so every pair follows the same steps. before marks the end of the prefix already placed in its final order. In each iteration, relink before -&gt; first -&gt; second -&gt; rest as before -&gt; second -&gt; first -&gt; rest, then advance before to first. This invariant keeps the processed prefix settled while preserving the unprocessed suffix.The loop runs only when two nodes remain. If the list has an odd length, its final unpaired node stays in place. The dummy is the only temporary node; the returned list contains the original nodes. The algorithm takes $O(N)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space./** * Definition for singly-linked list. * public class ListNode { * int val; * ListNode next; * ListNode() {} * ListNode(int val) { this.val = val; } * ListNode(int val, ListNode next) { this.val = val; this.next = next; } * } */class Solution { public ListNode swapPairs(ListNode head) { // The dummy gives the first pair a predecessor just like every later pair. ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head); ListNode before = dummy; // Invariant: nodes before `before` are already in their final order. while (before.next != null &amp;&amp; before.next.next != null) { ListNode first = before.next; ListNode second = first.next; // Relink the pair, preserving the remaining suffix. first.next = second.next; second.next = first; before.next = second; // Continue with the next pair after the two swapped nodes. before = first; } // A final unpaired node stays in place; no new list nodes are returned. return dummy.next; }}

title: LeetCode. 23. Merge k Sorted Lists
tags: Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, List, Merge k Sorted Lists
snippet: ProblemApproachKeep the current head of every non-empty input list in a min-heap. At each step, the heap contains exactly the smallest unmerged node from each list that still has nodes. Therefore, its minimum is the smallest node remaining across all lists and can be appended to the result. After removing that node, enqueue its successor before linking the removed node; saving the successor first keeps the unmerged input chain available while the node is reused.The result uses the original input nodes rather than allocating replacement nodes. A dummy head simplifies appending. When the heap becomes empty, explicitly set the final tail’s next to null so the result is terminated and cannot retain an old link that would create a cycle. An empty array or an array containing only null heads naturally returns null.For N total nodes and K input lists, each node is inserted into and removed from a heap at most once, with heap operations costing O(log K). The time complexity is O(N log K) and the auxiliary heap space is O(K).Javaimport java.util.PriorityQueue;/** * Definition for singly-linked list. * public class ListNode { * int val; * ListNode next; * ListNode() {} * ListNode(int val) { this.val = val; } * ListNode(int val, ListNode next) { this.val = val; this.next = next; } * } */class Solution { public ListNode mergeKLists(ListNode[] lists) { PriorityQueue&lt;ListNode&gt; minHeap = new PriorityQueue&lt;&gt;((a, b) -&gt; Integer.compare(a.val, b.val)); for (ListNode head : lists) { if (head != null) { minHeap.offer(head); } } ListNode dummy = new ListNode(); ListNode tail = dummy; while (!minHeap.isEmpty()) { ListNode node = minHeap.poll(); ListNode successor = node.next; if (successor != null) { minHeap.offer(successor); } tail.next = node; tail = node; } tail.next = null; return dummy.next; }}

title: LeetCode. 21. Merge Two Sorted Lists
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Merge Two Sorted Lists
snippet: LinkApproachUse a dummy head to simplify building the result, and keep a tail pointer at the last node appended. While both input lists are non-null, append the smaller current node and advance only the list that supplied it. The result is always sorted, and contains exactly the nodes consumed from the inputs in order. When one list ends, attach the other list’s remaining suffix; it is already sorted.The dummy node also handles empty inputs uniformly: if either input is null, the other list is returned unchanged, and if both are null, the result is null. No input nodes are copied; the result reuses every input node exactly once.For input lengths N and M, each node is visited once, so the time complexity is O(N + M). Apart from the fixed dummy node and pointers, the auxiliary space complexity is O(1).Java/** * Definition for singly-linked list. * public class ListNode { * int val; * ListNode next; * ListNode() {} * ListNode(int val) { this.val = val; } * ListNode(int val, ListNode next) { this.val = val; this.next = next; } * } */class Solution { public ListNode mergeTwoLists(ListNode list1, ListNode list2) { ListNode dummy = new ListNode(); ListNode tail = dummy; while (list1 != null &amp;&amp; list2 != null) { if (list1.val &lt;= list2.val) { tail.next = list1; list1 = list1.next; } else { tail.next = list2; list2 = list2.next; } tail = tail.next; } tail.next = (list1 != null) ? list1 : list2; return dummy.next; }}

title: LeetCode. 10. Regular Expression Matching
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Regular Expression Matching
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/regular-expression-matching/Dynamic programmingThis problem uses only two pattern operators: . matches exactly one arbitrary character, and * matches zero or more copies of the immediately preceding atom. Thus, * is handled together with the atom directly before it; it does not stand alone or apply to an earlier part of the pattern. The problem guarantees that every pattern is valid, so every * has a preceding atom.Let dp[i][j] mean that the first i characters of s match the first j characters of p. The result is dp[s.length()][p.length()]. The empty prefixes match, so dp[0][0] is true. An empty string can match a nonempty pattern only when its final atom-star pair is skipped: for each valid x* pair, dp[0][j] = dp[0][j - 2].For a pattern character other than *, it must match the current input character (either the same literal character or .), and the preceding prefixes must already match: dp[i][j] = matches(s[i - 1], p[j - 1]) &amp;&amp; dp[i - 1][j - 1].For an x* pair, there are two possibilities. It can match zero copies of x, leaving dp[i][j - 2]; or it can consume one matching input character and keep the same pattern pair available for further copies, requiring matches(s[i - 1], p[j - 2]) &amp;&amp; dp[i - 1][j].The table takes O(|s||p|) time and O(|s||p|) space.Javaclass Solution { public boolean isMatch(String s, String p) { int m = s.length(); int n = p.length(); boolean[][] dp = new boolean[m + 1][n + 1]; dp[0][0] = true; for (int j = 2; j &lt;= n; j++) { if (p.charAt(j - 1) == '*') { dp[0][j] = dp[0][j - 2]; } } for (int i = 1; i &lt;= m; i++) { for (int j = 1; j &lt;= n; j++) { char patternChar = p.charAt(j - 1); if (patternChar == '*') { char atom = p.charAt(j - 2); dp[i][j] = dp[i][j - 2] || (matches(s.charAt(i - 1), atom) &amp;&amp; dp[i - 1][j]); } else { dp[i][j] = matches(s.charAt(i - 1), patternChar) &amp;&amp; dp[i - 1][j - 1]; } } } return dp[m][n]; } private boolean matches(char input, char atom) { return atom == '.' || input == atom; }}

title: LeetCode. 20. Valid Parentheses
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Stack, Valid Parentheses
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-parentheses/ApproachScan the string from left to right while keeping unmatched opening brackets in a stack. Before processing each character, the stack contains exactly the opening brackets that have been seen but not yet matched, in their original order. Therefore, when a closing bracket appears, it must match the most recently seen opening bracket. If the stack is empty or the types do not match, the string is invalid. After the scan, the string is valid only if the stack is empty; otherwise, an opening bracket was left unmatched.The problem constraints guarantee that the string contains only ()[]{}. Each character is processed once, so the time complexity is O(N). In the worst case, all characters are opening brackets, so the auxiliary space complexity is O(N).Javaimport java.util.ArrayDeque;import java.util.Deque;class Solution { public boolean isValid(String s) { Deque&lt;Character&gt; stack = new ArrayDeque&lt;&gt;(); for (int i = 0; i &lt; s.length(); i++) { char c = s.charAt(i); if (c == '(' || c == '{' || c == '[') { stack.push(c); continue; } if (stack.isEmpty()) { return false; } char opener = stack.pop(); if ((c == ')' &amp;&amp; opener != '(') || (c == '}' &amp;&amp; opener != '{') || (c == ']' &amp;&amp; opener != '[')) { return false; } } return stack.isEmpty(); }}

title: LeetCode. 17. Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, DFS, Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
snippet: ProblemBacktrackingThe input contains digits from 2 through 9. Each digit maps directly to its phone-keypad letters. If the input is empty, there are no combinations, so return an empty list.The recursion processes one digit at a time. Its invariant is that, upon entering the call for index i, the StringBuilder contains exactly one selected letter for each of the first i digits, in order. For each letter mapped to the current digit, append that letter, recurse to the next index, and then delete the appended character before trying the next letter. At depth N, the prefix contains one letter per input digit, so save it as a completed combination.There are at most 4^N combinations, and copying each completed string takes O(N) time, giving output-sensitive worst-case time O(N * 4^N). The builder and recursion stack use O(N) auxiliary space, excluding the output list.Javaclass Solution { private static final String[] KEYPAD = { "", "", "abc", "def", "ghi", "jkl", "mno", "pqrs", "tuv", "wxyz" }; public List&lt;String&gt; letterCombinations(String digits) { List&lt;String&gt; answer = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(); if (digits.isEmpty()) { return answer; } backtrack(digits, 0, new StringBuilder(), answer); return answer; } private void backtrack(String digits, int index, StringBuilder prefix, List&lt;String&gt; answer) { if (index == digits.length()) { answer.add(prefix.toString()); return; } String letters = KEYPAD[digits.charAt(index) - '0']; for (int i = 0; i &lt; letters.length(); i++) { prefix.append(letters.charAt(i)); backtrack(digits, index + 1, prefix, answer); prefix.deleteCharAt(prefix.length() - 1); } }}

title: AtCoder Typical 90 021 — Come Back in One Piece
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Graph, SCC, Kosaraju's algorithm
snippet: [Link] https://AtCoder.jp/contests/typical90/tasks/typical90_uThis problem asks for the number of unordered pairs of distinct vertices that can reach each other. Two vertices are mutually reachable exactly when they belong to the same strongly connected component (SCC): every vertex in an SCC has a directed path to every other vertex in it.For each component of size s, all s * (s - 1) / 2 pairs qualify. We use iterative Kosaraju: the first depth-first search records vertices in finish order using explicit frames, and the second traverses the reversed graph in decreasing finish order to collect SCCs. Explicit stacks avoid Java call-stack overflow on deep graphs. The algorithm takes O(N + M) time and O(N + M) space.The input vertices are numbered from 1 through N. The parser accepts arbitrary whitespace between all integers.import java.io.*;import java.util.*;public class Main { static class FastScanner { private final InputStream in = System.in; private final byte[] buffer = new byte[1 &lt;&lt; 16]; private int ptr = 0, len = 0; int nextInt() throws IOException { int c; do { c = read(); } while (c &lt;= ' ' &amp;&amp; c != -1); int value = 0; while (c &gt; ' ') { value = value * 10 + c - '0'; c = read(); } return value; } private int read() throws IOException { if (ptr == len) { len = in.read(buffer); ptr = 0; if (len == -1) return -1; } return buffer[ptr++]; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { FastScanner fs = new FastScanner(); int n = fs.nextInt(); int m = fs.nextInt(); List&lt;Integer&gt;[] graph = new ArrayList[n + 1]; List&lt;Integer&gt;[] reverse = new ArrayList[n + 1]; for (int i = 1; i &lt;= n; i++) { graph[i] = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(); reverse[i] = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(); } for (int i = 0; i &lt; m; i++) { int from = fs.nextInt(); int to = fs.nextInt(); graph[from].add(to); reverse[to].add(from); } boolean[] visited = new boolean[n + 1]; int[] nextEdge = new int[n + 1]; int[] stack = new int[n]; int[] order = new int[n]; int orderSize = 0; for (int start = 1; start &lt;= n; start++) { if (visited[start]) continue; int top = 0; stack[0] = start; visited[start] = true; while (top &gt;= 0) { int v = stack[top]; if (nextEdge[v] &lt; graph[v].size()) { int to = graph[v].get(nextEdge[v]++); if (!visited[to]) { visited[to] = true; stack[++top] = to; } } else { order[orderSize++] = v; top--; } } } Arrays.fill(visited, false); long answer = 0; for (int i = orderSize - 1; i &gt;= 0; i--) { int start = order[i]; if (visited[start]) continue; int top = 0; int size = 0; stack[0] = start; visited[start] = true; while (top &gt;= 0) { int v = stack[top--]; size++; for (int to : reverse[v]) { if (!visited[to]) { visited[to] = true; stack[++top] = to; } } } answer += (long) size * (size - 1) / 2; } System.out.println(answer); }}

title: Graph theory. Strongly Connected Component(SCC)
tags: Graph theory, Algorithm, Strongly Connected Component, SCC, Tarjan's algorithm, Kosaraju's algorithm
snippet: Strongly Connected ComponentsIn a directed graph, a strongly connected component (SCC) is a maximal set of vertices in which every vertex is reachable from every other vertex. Reachability is mutual: for any two vertices u and v in the same SCC, there is a directed path from u to v and a directed path from v to u. A one-way path alone does not put its endpoints in the same component.Tarjan’s algorithmTarjan’s algorithm finds all SCCs in one depth-first traversal. The function below accepts an adjacency list: graph[u] contains the 0-based vertex indices reached by outgoing edges from u. It returns an array of components, each of which is an array of 0-based vertex indices. Component and vertex order are not significant.For each vertex, index records its discovery order and lowLink records the smallest discovery index reachable from it by following DFS-tree edges and, when applicable, one edge to a vertex still on the active stack. A tree edge propagates the child’s lowLink after that child is explored. A back edge to an active vertex uses that vertex’s index, not its lowLink; edges to vertices already removed from the stack are ignored. This on-stack rule prevents a completed SCC from incorrectly joining a later one.When lowLink[v] === index[v], v is the root of an SCC. Pop vertices from the stack through v; those popped vertices form one component. The outer loop starts DFS from every undiscovered vertex, so disconnected parts of the graph are included.function stronglyConnectedComponents(graph) { const n = graph.length; const index = Array(n).fill(-1); const lowLink = Array(n).fill(0); const onStack = Array(n).fill(false); const stack = []; const components = []; let nextIndex = 0; function visit(v) { index[v] = nextIndex; lowLink[v] = nextIndex; nextIndex += 1; stack.push(v); onStack[v] = true; for (const w of graph[v]) { if (index[w] === -1) { visit(w); lowLink[v] = Math.min(lowLink[v], lowLink[w]); } else if (onStack[w]) { lowLink[v] = Math.min(lowLink[v], index[w]); } } if (lowLink[v] === index[v]) { const component = []; let w; do { w = stack.pop(); onStack[w] = false; component.push(w); } while (w !== v); components.push(component); } } for (let v = 0; v &lt; n; v += 1) { if (index[v] === -1) visit(v); } return components;}The algorithm takes O(V + E) time and O(V) auxiliary space, where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of directed edges. The implementation is recursive, so its call depth can be O(V); extremely deep graphs may exceed the JavaScript runtime’s call-stack limit and may need an iterative implementation.

title: LeetCode. 19. Remove Nth Node From End of List
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Remove Nth Node From End of List
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list/Given the head of a singly linked list, remove its nth node from the end and return the head. The input guarantees that n is valid. Relink the existing nodes rather than copying their values.Use a dummy node before the head and two pointers, fast and slow. First advance fast by n links from the dummy, so the pointers have an n-node gap. Then move both pointers together until fast is the last node. At that point, slow is immediately before the node to remove; unlink it by assigning slow.next = slow.next.next.The dummy node supplies a predecessor even when the node to remove is the original head. Thus head removal uses the same unlinking step as every other position, and dummy.next is the resulting head. Since n is guaranteed valid, advancing fast by n links is safe.Time complexity is $O(N)$, and extra space complexity is $O(1)$./** * Definition for singly-linked list. * public class ListNode { * int val; * ListNode next; * ListNode() {} * ListNode(int val) { this.val = val; } * ListNode(int val, ListNode next) { this.val = val; this.next = next; } * } */class Solution { public ListNode removeNthFromEnd(ListNode head, int n) { ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head); ListNode fast = dummy; ListNode slow = dummy; // Keep fast n links ahead, then move both pointers in lockstep. for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { fast = fast.next; } while (fast.next != null) { fast = fast.next; slow = slow.next; } // slow is the predecessor, including when the original head is removed. slow.next = slow.next.next; return dummy.next; }}

title: De Moivre's formula
tags: Colleague Math, Complex Analysis
snippet:
StatementWrite a complex number in polar form as\[z=r(\cos	heta+i\sin	heta),\]where $r\ge 0$ is its modulus and $	heta$ is an argument measured in radians. For every integer $n$,\[z^n=r^n igl(\cos(n	heta)+i\sin(n	heta) igr).\]For $n&lt;0$, require $z
e 0$; for $n=0$, the expression is defined when $z
e 0$ as well. For positive $n$, the identity also holds at $z=0$.ProofEuler’s formula gives $z=re^{i	heta}$. Raising both sides to an integer power gives\[z^n=(re^{i	heta})^n=r^n e^{in	heta}=r^n igl(\cos(n	heta)+i\sin(n	heta) igr),\]using $e^{i\phi}=\cos\phi+i\sin\phi$. Equivalently, each multiplication by $z$ multiplies the modulus by $r$ and adds $	heta$ to the argument; after $n$ multiplications, these become $r^n$ and $n	heta$. The same rule extends to negative powers by taking reciprocals when $z
e0$.ExampleTaking $z=\cos(\pi/6)+i\sin(\pi/6)$ and $n=3$,\[z^3=\cos(3\pi/6)+i\sin(3\pi/6)=\cos(\pi/2)+i\sin(\pi/2)=i.\]The angles here are in radians.

title: LeetCode. 1. Two Sum
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Two Sum
snippet: ProblemApproachScan the array once from left to right. Before processing nums[i], the map contains each value seen at an earlier index and that value’s index. For the current value, look up its complement, target - nums[i]. If it is present, the stored index and i form the answer. Otherwise, store the current value and index for later elements.The map contains only earlier indices, so a match can never reuse the current element. LeetCode guarantees exactly one solution, so the scan will find and return that pair.The complement is computed as a long before looking it up. If it is outside the int range, it cannot equal any array value and is skipped; this avoids overflow in target - nums[i].Expected time complexity is O(N), with O(N) additional space.Javaimport java.util.HashMap;import java.util.Map;class Solution { public int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) { Map&lt;Integer, Integer&gt; earlierIndices = new HashMap&lt;&gt;(); for (int i = 0; i &lt; nums.length; i++) { long complement = (long) target - nums[i]; if (complement &gt;= Integer.MIN_VALUE &amp;&amp; complement &lt;= Integer.MAX_VALUE) { Integer earlierIndex = earlierIndices.get((int) complement); if (earlierIndex != null) { return new int[] { earlierIndex, i }; } } earlierIndices.put(nums[i], i); } throw new IllegalStateException("LeetCode guarantees exactly one solution"); }}

title: LeetCode 94. Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
snippet: ProblemApproachAn inorder traversal visits each node in left-node-right order. An explicit stack stores nodes whose left subtrees have not yet been fully processed. Starting at the root, descend as far left as possible and push each node. Then pop the next node, append its value, and move to its right child; repeat until both the current node and the stack are empty. This also returns an empty list when the root is null.The stack contains at most one root-to-leaf path, so the auxiliary space is O(H), where H is the tree height. Every node is pushed and popped once, giving O(N) time. The traversal only reads the tree and does not mutate any node.Java/** * Definition for a binary tree node. * public class TreeNode { * int val; * TreeNode left; * TreeNode right; * TreeNode() {} * TreeNode(int val) { this.val = val; } * TreeNode(int val, TreeNode left, TreeNode right) { * this.val = val; * this.left = left; * this.right = right; * } * } */class Solution { public List&lt;Integer&gt; inorderTraversal(TreeNode root) { List&lt;Integer&gt; result = new ArrayList&lt;&gt;(); ArrayDeque&lt;TreeNode&gt; stack = new ArrayDeque&lt;&gt;(); TreeNode current = root; while (current != null || !stack.isEmpty()) { while (current != null) { stack.push(current); current = current.left; } current = stack.pop(); result.add(current.val); current = current.right; } return result; }}

title: LeetCode. 540. Single Element in a Sorted Array
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Binary Search, Single Element in a Sorted Array
snippet: [Problem] https://leetcode.com/problems/single-element-in-a-sorted-array/In a sorted array, every value except the singleton appears exactly twice. Before the singleton, each pair starts at an even index; after it, the pair alignment shifts, so each pair starts at an odd index.At each iteration, align mid to the even index at the start of a pair. If nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1], that pair is intact and the singleton is to its right. Otherwise, the pair is disrupted at or before mid, so the singleton is at or to its left. This keeps the search interval focused on the half containing the singleton.The input is guaranteed to be nonempty, have odd length, and contain exactly one singleton. The loop converges to its index and returns its value. Binary search takes $O(\log N)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space.class Solution { public int singleNonDuplicate(int[] nums) { int low = 0, high = nums.length - 1; while (low &lt; high) { int mid = low + (high - low) / 2; if ((mid &amp; 1) == 1) mid--; if (nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1]) { low = mid + 2; } else { high = mid; } } return nums[low]; }}

title: LeetCode. 461. Hamming Distance
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/hamming-distance/XOR sets a bit to 1 exactly where the corresponding bits of x and y differ, so x ^ y marks every differing position. Integer.bitCount counts those set bits, which is the Hamming distance.Java integers have a fixed width of 32 bits, so the operation takes $O(1)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space.class Solution { public int hammingDistance(int x, int y) { // XOR sets a bit exactly where the two inputs differ. // bitCount counts those differing positions. return Integer.bitCount(x ^ y); }}

title: BOJ 11659 — Range Sum Query 4
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Prefix Sum, Coding Interview, BOJ, Range Sum Query 4
snippet: BOJ 11659: Range Sum Query 4For an array, build a prefix-sum array where prefix[0] = 0 andprefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + value[i]. The sum of an inclusive range[a, b] is prefix[b] - prefix[a - 1]. The input positions are 1-indexed,so the prefix indices account for converting them to Java’s 0-indexed array.The prefix array is built in O(N) time, and each of the M queries isanswered in O(1), for O(N + M) total time and O(N) space. ABufferedReader and StringTokenizer read tokens across arbitrarywhitespace, and a StringBuilder collects the answers before output.import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.IOException;import java.io.InputStreamReader;import java.util.StringTokenizer;public class Main { private static BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); private static StringTokenizer tokenizer; private static int nextInt() throws IOException { while (tokenizer == null || !tokenizer.hasMoreTokens()) { tokenizer = new StringTokenizer(reader.readLine()); } return Integer.parseInt(tokenizer.nextToken()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { int n = nextInt(); int m = nextInt(); int[] prefix = new int[n + 1]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; n; i++) { prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nextInt(); } StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i &lt; m; i++) { int a = nextInt(); int b = nextInt(); output.append(prefix[b] - prefix[a - 1]).append('\n'); } System.out.print(output); }}

title: LeetCode. 53. Maximum Subarray
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Maximum Subarray
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-subarray/ApproachThe input array is guaranteed to be non-empty. Scan it once while tracking the largest sum of a subarray that must end at the current index (ending) and the largest sum seen anywhere (best). At each element, either extend the previous subarray or start a new one at the current element:ending = max(nums[i], ending + nums[i])After updating ending, update best if the new ending sum is larger. Initializing both values to nums[0] ensures every candidate is a non-empty subarray. In particular, when all values are negative, the algorithm returns the largest (least negative) single-element subarray instead of incorrectly returning zero.The invariant is that after processing index i, ending is the maximum sum of any non-empty subarray ending at i, and best is the maximum sum of any non-empty subarray in the processed prefix.Time complexity is O(N) and extra space complexity is O(1).Javaclass Solution { public int maxSubArray(int[] nums) { int ending = nums[0]; int best = nums[0]; for (int i = 1; i &lt; nums.length; i++) { ending = Math.max(nums[i], ending + nums[i]); best = Math.max(best, ending); } return best; }}

title: LeetCode. 13. Roman to Integer
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Roman to Integer
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/roman-to-integer/Left-to-right scanIn a canonical Roman numeral, a symbol is subtracted only when it is immediately followed by a larger symbol. Thus IV is -1 + 5 = 4, while a symbol not in such a subtractive pair contributes its usual value. Comparing each symbol with its next symbol applies this rule directly. The loop invariant is that after each iteration, sum equals the signed contribution of every symbol processed so far: a symbol contributes negatively exactly when its next symbol is larger. Canonical notation guarantees that these local contributions express the numeral’s value. The final symbol has no successor and is always added.The input is guaranteed to be a canonical Roman numeral representing a value from 1 through 3999, so no validation is needed.Javaclass Solution { public int romanToInt(String s) { int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i &lt; s.length(); i++) { int current = valueOf(s.charAt(i)); if (i + 1 &lt; s.length() &amp;&amp; current &lt; valueOf(s.charAt(i + 1))) { sum -= current; } else { sum += current; } } return sum; } private int valueOf(char symbol) { switch (symbol) { case 'I': return 1; case 'V': return 5; case 'X': return 10; case 'L': return 50; case 'C': return 100; case 'D': return 500; default: return 1000; // M; the input is guaranteed to be valid. } }}Each symbol is examined a constant number of times, so the running time is $O(N)$ for a string of length $N$. The scan uses $O(1)$ extra space.

title: LeetCode. 83. Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, LinkedList, Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list/ApproachBecause the list is sorted, equal values are adjacent. Keep a pointer at the last retained node. If its next node has the same value, bypass that next node; otherwise, advance the pointer. At each step, the list from the head through the pointer contains exactly one node for every distinct value processed so far, in sorted order. The final retained node is the original last node, whose next is already null, so the result has no cycle.Each node is examined once, so the time complexity is O(N). The algorithm reuses the input nodes and uses O(1) extra space./** * Definition for singly-linked list. * public class ListNode { * int val; * ListNode next; * ListNode() {} * ListNode(int val) { this.val = val; } * ListNode(int val, ListNode next) { this.val = val; this.next = next; } * } */class Solution { public ListNode deleteDuplicates(ListNode head) { ListNode node = head; while (node != null &amp;&amp; node.next != null) { if (node.val == node.next.val) { node.next = node.next.next; } else { node = node.next; } } return head; }}

title: AtCoder. 019 Pick Two(6)
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, AtCoder, Pick Two
snippet: [Link] https://AtCoder.jp/contests/typical90/tasks/typical90_simport java.util.*;import java.io.*;public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { BufferedReader bf = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); int n = atoi(bf.readLine()); String[] split = bf.readLine().split(" "); int[] a = new int[2*n]; int[][] dp = new int[2*n][2*n]; for(int i = 0; i &lt; 2 * n; i++) a[i] = atoi(split[i]); for(int i = 0; i &lt; 2 * n; i++) { for(int j = (((i%2)&amp;1)==0) ? 1 : 0; j &lt; i; j+=2) { int min = Integer.MAX_VALUE; for(int k = j; k &lt; i; k+=2) min = Math.min(min, Math.abs(a[i] - a[k]) + (k &gt; j ? dp[j][k - 1] : 0) + (k + 1 &lt; i - 1 ? dp[k + 1][i - 1] : 0)); dp[j][i] = min; } } System.out.println(dp[0][2 * n - 1]); } static int atoi(String s) { return Integer.parseInt(s); }}

title: LeetCode. 14. Longest Common Prefix
tags: Code Block, Code Snippet, Java, Algorithm, Coding Interview, LeetCode, Longest Common Prefix
snippet: [Link] https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-common-prefix/ApproachScan the first string from left to right. At each position, compare its character with the character at the same position in every other string. The first mismatch ends the shared prefix, so return the part of the first string before that position.Before comparing a position, check whether each other string is long enough to contain it. If it is shorter, the common prefix ends at its length. The scan never indexes past a string’s end, and the first string itself is the candidate prefix, so no separate prefix buffer is needed.The algorithm inspects at most the characters covered by the shortest string across the input, for O(S) total inspected characters, where S is the sum of the lengths of all strings. It uses O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the returned substring.class Solution { public String longestCommonPrefix(String[] strs) { if (strs.length == 0) { return ""; } String first = strs[0]; for (int i = 0; i &lt; first.length(); i++) { char current = first.charAt(i); for (int j = 1; j &lt; strs.length; j++) { if (i &gt;= strs[j].length() || strs[j].charAt(i) != current) { return first.substring(0, i); } } } return first; }}
